World.title: Say cheese: A guide to 5 iconic Mexican quesos and the regions that produce them
World.content:
In Mexico, an endless debate spills across social media and enlists everyone from linguists and historians to cooks and passionate eaters: What belongs in a quesadilla? While cheese is an optional topping for many Mexican dishes — from tacos and tortas to chilaquiles and sopes — there is one contentious item that, depending on who you ask, is non-negotiable.

Now, we are not here to solve the great quesadilla debate, but unveiling the passion behind it shows just how central cheese is to Mexican gastronomy. From north to south, every region has crafted its own variety of queso tailored to its local heritage. Here are five of Mexico’s most iconic cheeses:

Queso Oaxaca (or quesillo)

The cheese at the very heart of the debate — and a cornerstone of Mexican street food — is queso Oaxaca, locally known as quesillo. It is celebrated for its soft, buttery texture and its exceptional meltability over high heat, whether tucked into a sope, folded inside a quesadilla or pressed into a torta.

What differentiates quesillo from other cheeses is its distinct curdling method: It is hand-stretched into long, milky strands and wound into a ribboned ball. Achieving this pliable texture relies on warm preparation techniques that keep the cheese flexible enough to stretch and interlace without breaking.

Quesillo is indispensable in Mexican households as it can turn a simple tortilla (corn or flour) into a quick homemade quesadilla for dinner, transform refried beans and bread into crispy, freshly baked molletes, or serve as a quick, savory snack eaten straight from the fridge.

Originally from: Oaxaca

Queso de cincho

Loosely translated as “cinch cheese,” queso de cincho originates in the central state of Morelos and the southwestern state of Guerrero. Its name refers to the rigid mold used during pressing, which is bound tightly with woven ixtle palm fibers (the same durable rope material used in traditional horse tack and saddlery).

Also known as queso prensado estilo Guerrero, this firm, aged cheese carries a strong aroma and is typically rubbed with a paste of dried guajillo chiles. While frequently crumbled over enchiladas or chilaquiles, one of its most traditional preparations is simmered directly in salsa as a guisado. Thanks to its dense consistency and high protein content, it serves as a substantial centerpiece. Better yet, its low moisture content allows it to age naturally at room temperature for up to a year without spoiling.

Originally from: Guerrero and Morelos

Queso asadero

Just like quesillo, queso asadero is popular due to its creamy, melty texture and the gastronomic possibilities it offers. This type of cheese has similar uses to queso Oaxaca; it can be used in quesadillas, and it is common at northern cookouts, paired with a great steak. If you’ve been to one of those, the name “asadero” might sound familiar — it comes from the word asado (grilled), a clue on how to enjoy this cheese.

Originally from: Chihuahua

Queso fresco

View this post on Instagram A post shared by 𝑪𝒂𝒔𝒂𝒏𝒅𝒓𝒂 𝑺𝒂𝒍𝒊𝒏𝒂𝒔 🤠🌵 (@yo_soy_casandra)

Queso fresco is a crumbly, soft cheese that is high in moisture and protein. Due to its short aging process (which is where the name fresco — or fresh — comes from), it is difficult to keep for long periods. It must always be kept refrigerated and consumed within approximately two weeks.

Regarding its preparation and curdling, queso fresco is quite versatile, as it can be made with cow’s milk, goat’s milk or a blend of both. In contrast to meltable cheeses, queso fresco does not work as a quesadilla filling, but it is the perfect topping for side dishes, whether sprinkled over a salad, street corn or refried beans.

Originally from: Chihuahua

Queso Menonita

View this post on Instagram A post shared by ¡ah Chihuahua! (@ahchihuahua)

Last but not least is Mennonite cheese, a famous variety that also comes from the northern region of the country. As its name reveals, it originates from a specific community: the Mennonites. Groups of Mennonite immigrants arrived in Mexico during the 1920s, and their cattle-ranching techniques thrived in the north.

Mennonite communities settled mainly in the drylands of Chihuahua and relied on dairy products, especially cheese, for sustenance. Nowadays — although the name remains — this smooth, buttery cheese is no longer exclusively made by Mennonite communities. You can find it melting inside chiles rellenos, on Mennonite-style pizzas or in choriqueso (a dish of melted cheese combined with seasoned chorizo).

Originally from: Chihuahua

Cheese has been a companion to Mexican cuisine for centuries. One key to understanding its strong northern presence is the geographic distribution of agriculture and livestock in Mexico. As you travel from south to north, the climate becomes drier, making the land better suited for cattle ranching than crop cultivation.

It is no surprise, then, that cheese became a fundamental pillar of northern Mexico’s economy and gastronomy.

After all, what would a northern carne asada be without quesadillas (con queso)?

Lydia Leija is a linguist, journalist and visual storyteller. She has directed three feature films, and her audiovisual work has been featured in national and international media. She’s been part of National Geographic, Muy Interesante and Cosmopolitan.

World.title: Does having dual citizenship have any downsides?
World.content:
In 2016, my wife and I embarked on a road trip together across central Mexico — starting on Jalisco’s Pacific Coast and, over a month later, ending up on the Gulf Coast of Veracruz with innumerable side quests along the way in Michoacán, Guanajuato, Querétaro, Hidalgo, Mexico City, Estado de México and Puebla.

It wasn’t our first time in Mexico. We had, after all, spent our lifetimes visiting our extended families in Mexico as the children of immigrants.

But now we were able to see it on our own terms, as independent adults with our own incomes to spend and itineraries to plan. We rediscovered the country through our own eyes.

That summer, we had a revelation: We wanted to live in Mexico.

Three years later, in 2019, we prepared a similar trek around the southern part of the country, beginning in Oaxaca’s capital, then winding our way through mountain towns en route to the coast on a colectivo. Months prior, we had left our jobs as high school teachers with the intent to live in Mexico long term. Then, COVID-19 happened while we were staying in Mexico City’s central Narvarte Poniente neighborhood.

It was an uncertain and frightening time to be traveling. We ultimately decided, as U.S. citizens with a travel visa, to return to California after nearly half a year away. As tourists, we would have violated our 180-day limit and didn’t want to risk overstaying; had we been dual citizens, we would have had less pressure to return so suddenly.

Navigating the consulate and paperwork

But we hadn’t given up on our ambitions to live in Mexico as Mexican Americans. Shortly after returning to the San Francisco region, I began my application process to become a dual Mexican citizen.

In my case, I had a major advantage: My mom never rescinded her Mexican citizenship, despite having lived in the United States for more than 30 years after immigrating as a young woman. When she eventually moved back to Mexico, it inspired me to follow her southward. Through her, my direct path to citizenship had already been laid out.

The process took me a couple of years, though it could have been completed much more swiftly. I took my time and wasn’t in a rush during the pandemic. I visited different consulates in California, and after waiting in many lines and talking to many people, I gathered all of the documents — most importantly, proof of my mother’s citizenship and birth certificate — and approvals.

Then, it happened: I had become a Mexican citizen, and I had my Mexican passport. (I would eventually get my INE, but I opted to do it in Mexico, rather than at any Mexican consulate in the U.S.).

My wife had a trickier path. Her Mexican-born father’s documents had a typo. Therefore, some of his documents didn’t exactly match. If you aren’t yet familiar with the distress an aberrant punctuation mark can trigger in the imperfect machinery of Mexican bureaucracy, I pray you never have to.

Ultimately, my wife was forced to hire a specialist who helps Mexican descendants obtain their Mexican citizenship — it was frictionless and worth the price. To date, we highly recommend it for anyone who has the funding or has experienced any complications with the process.

A historic surge in binational applicants

During that time, we weren’t alone in our journeys toward Mexican citizenship. Many of our Mexican American friends had expressed a desire to do the same, and in some cases, a few had already started their processes as well. In fact, dual citizenship applications — particularly for the U.S.-born descendants of Mexican immigrants — are reaching a historic apex. De Los, a Latino-focused branch of the Los Angeles Times, recently reported that “Between 2024 and 2025, registrations for Mexican citizenship skyrocketed by 161% at the Los Angeles consulate.”

The trend is universal throughout the U.S. In Boise, Idaho, reports indicate a rise in applicants due to Mexico’s law change in 2023, which simplified the route to dual citizenship for anyone with at least one Mexican-born parent. Combined with the ongoing pressures of xenophobic turmoil, immigration raids and other sociopolitical factors, more people are looking to gain a sense of security and connection on both sides of the border through binational citizenship.

The benefits of dual citizenship are certainly ample: Traveling as a dual citizen offers financial breaks and accessibility perks (there are fewer foreign fees to be paid at Mexican airports and museums, for example); purchasing property in Mexico involves fewer legal hurdles; and at large, it grants unrestricted freedoms on both sides of the border, which is an ultimate privilege.

The unexpected costs of double bureaucracy

But that’s where things can get a little complicated, depending on your plans and lifestyle. In my case, I don’t use my Mexican passport solely for a beach getaway once a year; I live and work in Mexico as a dual citizen, with employers and responsibilities in both countries, and the implications are different.

Vehicle registration in California expired and needs to be updated in person? Guess who’s flying back for a visit to the California Department of Motor Vehicles? Navigating Mexico’s monthly tax payments? Might require a tax accountant. Of course, each scenario comes with a cost, and many life lessons.

When I applied for dual citizenship, I wasn’t necessarily thinking about those realities, or how I would have to pay and renew double the amount of things as someone fully integrated into two federal systems. Of course, in retrospect it makes complete sense. But it’s not the sort of thing that a bright-eyed applicant has at the forefront of their mind while pursuing dual citizenship — nor is it the kind of thing that parents or friends who are encouraging dual citizenship are thinking about, either.

Political debates and balancing two worlds

The issue of dual citizenship has even caused some political strife. Just weeks ago, President Claudia Sheinbaum proposed a ban on dual citizens being able to reach the highest levels of office within Mexico’s borders. “Why have dual nationality if you’re going to represent the people of Mexico?” she rhetorically posed. The bill has been criticized by the Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI) as a discriminatory human rights violation.

However, for the average person who doesn’t intend to run for the Mexican presidency, dual citizens generally don’t have much to shy away from. If you plan to work in both countries as a dual citizen, be prepared to pay the taxes (literally and metaphorically). If you don’t plan to work in Mexico for Mexican-based companies, you can simply declare your non-working status in Mexico when registering for your INE, and your biggest potential taxation headaches will disappear — at least in one of the two countries.

The benefits

For all of its potential downsides, there are double the benefits. On days when I enter the U.S. through California airports and switch over to using English with my U.S. passport, it feels like I’m home. I’m just as happy and relieved as soon as I arrive back in Mexico, activate my Spanish mode, and show my Mexican passport.

As someone who grew up around many undocumented Mexican immigrants in California, I don’t take that lightly. And I use it to constantly toggle my way between both worlds, as my fullest self.

Alan Chazaro is the author of “These Spaceships Weren’t Built For Us” (Tia Chucha Press, 2026), “Notes from the Eastern Span of the Bay Bridge” (Ghost City Press, 2021), “Piñata Theory” (Black Lawrence Press, 2020), and “This Is Not a Frank Ocean Cover Album” (Black Lawrence Press, 2019). He is a graduate of June Jordan’s Poetry for the People program at UC Berkeley and was selected as a Lawrence Ferlinghetti Poetry Fellow at the University of San Francisco. His work can be found in NPR, The Guardian, SLAM, GQ, L.A. Times, and more. He is currently based in Veracruz.

World.title: ‘A Pilgrimage Across Cultures’: Tamanna Bembenek on finding her third space in Mexico
World.content:
A couple of decades ago, I became fascinated by the concept of the “third place,” which Howard Schultz, then CEO of Starbucks, helped make popular. The idea came from sociologist Ray Oldenburg: a gathering place outside home and work. Maybe it was all marketing, but Starbucks wanted to define its cafés as neutral ground — a place to meet a friend, study or socialize without the usual expectations of home or work. Starbucks was never quite that place for me, but I remained fascinated by the concept. At the time, I interpreted it as a judgment-free space. As I grew older, the term stuck with me but I began to discover another meaning for myself — less about a place to go and more about the freedom to simply be. That is a feeling I have come to call “my third space.” Let me explain what I mean.

In the last few years, I’ve been thinking a lot about the concept in the context of belonging. I’ve always felt fortunate to have lived and worked in multiple countries, because it let me cherry-pick the best aspects and values from different cultures — and do so in a uniquely American way. Individuality is a value I’ve fiercely cherished, yet that same fierceness has made me feel more alone in recent years.

As the political divide has grown in the U.S., I felt I had to pick a political side to satisfy a psychological need to belong with a group of friends or family. As time passed, my identity became tethered to a party rather than to the values it claimed to represent. Social media compounded this, sorting everyone into ever-narrower boxes: age bracket, income bracket, zip code, follower count, which side of a hashtag someone landed on, or generational labels — Gen Alpha, Gen Z, millennials, Gen X, baby boomers, and I’m sure I’ve missed a few. It felt increasingly claustrophobic. Instead of feeling free to choose the values and characteristics that would nurture my own identity as a good human first — regardless of any other labels — I felt I had to fit into someone else’s box, under a category they had defined. Add geopolitical craziness and the current noise around artificial intelligence (AI), including claims that there is a 10% chance that AI will “kill all humans,” and I started feeling not only alone but increasingly anxious and hopeless!

So, I started reading books and listening to podcasts to figure out the root cause of this feeling and how to remedy it. I was already dedicating quality time to pursuing art but increasingly, I also found myself drawn to ancient history — Roman, Egyptian, Indian, Mesoamerican, just to start with. I noticed that exploring stories about ancient civilizations made me feel less alone. It felt soothing. Whether I was reading history or the myths woven through it, I was searching for common themes, a connection, a sense of belonging. There’s a timeless quality to such stories that reminds us of our own mortality and, paradoxically, makes us feel less alone in facing it.

Slowly, I found myself weaving these stories into my art through the use of icons, symbols and allegory. I started visualizing and composing art in my mind — integrating these concepts with my love and knowledge of art history and modern art, my reverence for the ancient craft of handwoven textiles, and my deep interest in astronomy and life sciences.

I have to admit that my current environment is what made all of this possible. Living in Mexico gave me the space I needed: regardless of nationality, identity, or age, I could simply live and let live. Maybe it helps to be geographically so close to the country I truly love and yet not feel so boxed in. Slowly, I began to understand that I wasn’t looking for a place where I could fit in. I was looking for the freedom to belong to something purposeful as I continue to grow as a person — my Indian heritage, my American values, and my old soul that keeps drawing me towards unfamiliar, ancient worlds — and perhaps to the wisdom and spirituality within them. Living in Mexico gave me the freedom to explore those connections, and painting became a medium to express that.

Allow me to show you what I mean, figuratively.

To create is human

Through trial and error, I have discovered that the antidote to my anxiety is not a massage or a spa day or a beach vacation (though they help from time to time) — it is creativity. Creating art in this way — finding connections between ancient cultures — has made me feel whole again, like I am part of something bigger. The more I paint, the more I realize how central creativity is to being human. That’s what my art is really about. There’s a narrative, a thought, a meaning behind every piece — observations, symbolic connections, and questions drawn from books and podcasts on history, archaeology, anthropology and astronomy. There are no political messages. Just a personal journey, trying to make sense of the world I live in today. Creativity is a process, not an outcome: It is a place where I lose my sense of time, immerse myself fully, get stumped, get frustrated, and still come out energized, rooted, grounded. In that space, I stop performing for others and follow my own curiosity.

Maybe that is why creativity makes me feel whole. I don’t have to settle into a single version of my identity. Pueblo life in Mexico, my American individuality, and the ancient civilizations that shape us all can coexist instead of competing. I can keep growing, changing, transforming — staying a “work in progress.” Creativity grants me that permission when society won’t. And while each painting begins with my own vision, it is also an invitation for the viewer to make it their own. You don’t have to see what I see or arrive at the same answers. That is the freedom I have found in my third space: I can be rooted in who I am and still have room to become someone new. Today, I am enough but I am not yet done growing.

A third space you can visit

That sense of wholeness — maybe even greatness — is exactly what I hope visitors feel walking through my upcoming show. If this speaks to you, please come see it in person: I have a collaborative exhibition with Mexican artist Miguel Cuauhtémoc called “A Pilgrimage Across Cultures,” running Nov. 1-15 at Galería Torres del Reloj in Polanco, Mexico City. Miguel grew up immersed in the symbols and rituals of ancient Mexico, and I grew up surrounded by the colors and deities of India. Separately, we both kept arriving at the same recurring image, the third eye, which we each use to explore higher consciousness. Neither of us knew the other was painting it until we saw each other’s work. That discovery felt like another kind of belonging — a connection we had painted before we had even spoken about it.

If you’re in town, please stop by and say hello. And if you’d like to browse the fuller portfolio first, here’s the link: www.tamannabembenek.com.

I’ve written about my personal journey at length elsewhere, if you want to 

Tamanna Bembenek was born in India, studied and worked in the U.S. and now lives in Mexico with her husband, Travis. They are the co-owners of Mexico News Daily.

World.title: Sheinbaum meets with US business leaders and ambassador amid controversy over US-backed police academy
World.content:
Listen to this article

During a week in which she has questioned intrusive U.S. security policies, President Claudia Sheinbaum met with U.S. business leaders at the National Palace, but avoided discussing security initiatives with U.S. Ambassador Ronald Johnson who was in attendance.

Sheinbaum said Thursday’s meeting with the U.S. Chamber of Commerce and the American Chamber of Commerce of Mexico (AmCham) addressed issues related to the investment climate in Mexico, adding that she will address her concerns with Johnson at a later date.

“We focused on responding to the companies’ concerns, explaining the controversial new revenue law, discussing requests regarding trade and promoting the favorable environment for business investment in Mexico,” she said.

Also in attendance were the president of Mexico’s Business Coordinating Council, José Medina Mora, and the coordinator of the Advisory Council for Regional Economic Development and Relocation, Altagracia Gómez Sierra.

For its part, AmCham expressed interest in broader security issues, investment and greater private sector participation.

AmCham president Óscar del Cueto said his organization is eager for greater collaboration between the Mexican government and private enterprise, while also citing issues such as security, investment and greater private sector participation.

Several investment agreements were finalized (to be announced at a later date) and the U.S. contingent was given a detailed update on Plan México, Sheinbaum’s strategy for economic development, industrialization and regional growth.

The meeting took place amid an ongoing review of the Mexico-U.S. trade relationship as outlined in the U.S.-Mexico-Canada Agreement (USMCA). AmCham has publicly stated that the USMCA should be used to deepen regional integration and preserve the competitiveness of the economies of Mexico, the United States and Canada.

Del Cueto insists the trade scenario presents a key opportunity for Mexico if the United States goes through a new stage of growth and industrialization and China loses dynamism.

“I firmly believe that next year we could be returning to the topic of nearshoring as the hot topic,” he said.

While Sheinbaum preferred discussing plans to allow for increased investment and greater North American productive integration, the kerfuffle involving Ambassador Johnson was a hot topic with the media.

After participating in a groundbreaking ceremony for an International Police Training Academy in the state of Querétaro on Oct. 2, Johnson — and Governor Mauricio Kuri — have faced criticism over the apparent failure to obtain federal authorization as required by law.

Sheinbaum publicly questioned the project several times, asserting that state governments cannot forge international security agreements or launch such academies without federal and Foreign Ministry authorization.

While clarifying that Mexico is not fundamentally against international cooperation, Sheinbaum explicitly demanded “cooperation with dignity and transparency” rather than “subordination,” adding that it is imperative that federal frameworks not be bypassed.

During a meeting with legislators on Thursday, Security Minister Omar García Harfuch addressed Mexico’s concerns about foreign interference in security matters, insisting that bilateral cooperation is subject to the provisions of Mexican law.

Sheinbaum said Johnson has agreed to meet soon with Foreign Affairs Minister Roberto Velasco to discuss the police academy and other issues related to security and the border.

With reports from Informador, Milenio, El Heraldo de México and Heraldo USA

World.title: Simon, strengthening rapidly, could hit Jalisco or Colima as a major hurricane this weekend
World.content:
Hurricane Simon strengthened into a Category 2 storm Friday as authorities prepared for possible landfall in Jalisco or Colima — potentially bringing catastrophic winds, dangerous storm surge and flooding to Mexico on the heels of Hurricane Polo last week.

Forecasters expected the Pacific storm to become a major hurricane Friday evening and reach Category 4 strength Saturday, with sustained winds of 230 km/h (145 mph), according to a Friday morning advisory from the U.S. National Hurricane Center (NHC).

At 3 p.m. Mexico City time, the storm had maximum sustained winds of 165 km/h (105 mph) and was about 315 kilometers south of Manzanillo, Colima, moving northwest at 4 km/h (2 mph).

The eye of the storm is forecast to turn north and pass very near or over Mexico’s west-central coast late Saturday or Sunday. Tropical storm conditions are expected to carry through Saturday morning, followed by hurricane conditions Saturday evening or Sunday.

Simon could become the second hurricane to make landfall in Mexico this Pacific season, following Polo, which struck Baja California Sur on Sept. 28 and Sonora on Sept. 29.

Simon’s precise track remains uncertain. The NHC said the storm could weaken rapidly or dissipate if its center moves inland. If its core stays offshore, it could continue north as a hurricane.

A hurricane warning issued by Mexico’s National Water Commission (Conagua) remains in effect from Punta San Telmo, Michoacán, to Punta Mita, Nayarit — points roughly 475 kilometers (295 miles) apart by road. A hurricane watch extends north to San Blas, Nayarit, while a tropical storm watch extends south to Lázaro Cárdenas, Michoacán.

Dangerous storm surge could strike the coast and nearby inland areas, accompanied by large, destructive waves. Rainfall could trigger life-threatening flooding and mudslides, particularly on steep terrain.

Simon could bring 20 to 38 centimeters (8 to 15 inches) of rain across parts of southwestern Mexico through Sunday, with isolated totals of 64 centimeters (25 inches) in Michoacán, Colima, Jalisco and Nayarit, according to the hurricane center.

Laura Velázquez, Mexico’s national civil protection coordinator, said authorities Friday would establish command centers in Puerto Vallarta, Cihuatlán and Manzanillo.

Authorities began evacuations in El Rebalse, a community in Jalisco that is vulnerable to flooding from the Marabasco River. Seventy residents left on their own and 10 were moved to a shelter, Reuters reported.

Schools in 22 Jalisco municipalities suspended classes Friday and Monday.

Meanwhile, Hurricane Isaias, a Category 3 storm, was churning through the Gulf of Mexico, with landfall in the U.S. expected Friday evening, according to the hurricane center. No landfall in Mexico is forecast.

With reports from El Sol de México, Reuters and La Silla Rota

World.title: MND Local Puerto Vallarta: Mariachis, murals, drainage and demolition
World.content:
This week, Puerto Vallarta announced it will host a national children’s mariachi competition to promote this iconic Mexican musical style. Additionally, the Vallarta Institute of Culture issued a call for artists interested in decorating the walls of a local cemetery, and drainage work is expected to cause traffic disruptions on one of the city’s main thoroughfares.

Meanwhile, the Punta Paraíso tourism megaproject, planned for a stretch of beach in San Pancho, is set to be demolished due to environmental concerns.

Here are some of Puerto Vallarta’s top news stories.

Children’s and youth mariachi competition to be held in Puerto Vallarta

Puerto Vallarta will host the fourth Children’s and Youth Mariachi Competition Oct. 14-16, marking the first time the event takes place outside Guadalajara.

Featuring 18 groups from various regions of Jalisco, the competition seeks to foster the training of new generations of musicians while preserving the mariachi tradition.

Ten groups will participate in the intermediate category and eight in the advanced category. Activities will begin Oct. 14 with a masterclass at the La Lija Cultural Center. In the evening, the groups will perform in the opening gala at the Arcos del Malecón.

The jury will evaluate musical execution, performance quality, ensemble, intonation and adherence to mariachi tradition to select the finalist groups.

The finals will be held Oct. 16, starting at 6 p.m., at the Teatro Vallarta. Before the awards ceremony, all 18 participating groups will perform together.

Calling all muralists to decorate a cemetery for Day of the Dead

The Vallarta Institute of Culture is inviting artists to participate in an initiative to create 10 murals on the walls of the Municipal Pantheon in the 5 de Diciembre neighborhood.

The initiative, dubbed “Recuérdame” (Remember Me), aims to transform these spaces into public art galleries that reflect local identity and contribute to revitalizing the urban environment.

Proposals must draw inspiration from figures, traditions, flora, fauna and Puerto Vallarta’s local culture reinterpreted through the symbolism of Day of the Dead.

Applicants must submit their proposals Oct. 6-19; artist selection will take place Oct. 20. A committee will select 10 artists who must work on the murals Oct. 23-29.

Candidates must also submit a digital portfolio containing a maximum of five previous works demonstrating their experience in muralism. The portfolio must be submitted in PDF format.

Selected applicants will receive a cash prize of 7,000 pesos (US $368) upon completion of the mural.

For additional information about the application process, click here.

Demolition ordered for structures at Punta Paraíso complex in San Pancho

A federal court upheld an order for the partial demolition of the Punta Paraíso real estate development along the beach in San Pancho, Nayarit, following years of legal disputes over environmental irregularities.

The company must restore 1,466 square meters (about 15,780 square feet) of land reclaimed from the sea to its original state by demolishing unauthorized structures, and pay a fine of 96,220 pesos (US $5,300). The ruling also mandates the forfeiture to the government of the buildings known as Tower 1 and Tower 2.

The case also led to allegations against Roberto Rodríguez Medrano, the acting head of the Federal Attorney General’s Office for Environmental Protection (Profepa) in Nayarit. Former legislator Ismael Duñalds Ventura claims that the official endorsed the project’s environmental studies in 2018, when he led the Ministry of Environment and Natural Resources in Nayarit.

The concession permitted only recreational and ornamental activities, not commercial exploitation. A Profepa inspection launched in December 2021 confirmed the construction work that resulted in the sanctions.

Profepa head Mariana Boy Tamborrell described the ruling as a victory for the community and for the protection of the coastal ecosystem.

Drainage work at Las Palmas Park begins

The Potable Water, Drainage and Sewerage System (SEAPAL) in Puerto Vallarta has begun sanitary infrastructure rehabilitation work in the Parque Las Palmas neighborhood and along Avenida México — a project expected to last approximately six weeks and result in partial traffic closures.

The construction corresponds to the second phase of work on the area’s drainage system. It entails replacing 66 meters (about 216 feet) of pipeline, increasing conveyance capacity and creating a new alternative for wastewater discharge.

Furthermore, this project reinforces the measures SEAPAL Vallarta is taking to address and prevent issues related to sanitation infrastructure — following recent problems in the Versalles neighborhood — by increasing conveyance capacity and improving wastewater management options in this part of the city.

The construction work will cause intermittent restrictions at the intersection of México and Las Palmas avenues; therefore, motorists traveling through the area should anticipate potential disruptions. SEAPAL asked residents and drivers to take precautions, heed warning signs and follow the instructions of municipal traffic officers.

Gabriela Solís is a Mexican lawyer turned full-time writer. She was born and raised in Guadalajara and covers business, culture, lifestyle and travel for Mexico News Daily. You can follow her lifestyle blog Dunas y Palmeras.

World.title: BTS Asks Lima Fans to Shun Hotel Before 10 October Show
World.content:
The Larcomar complex and the Miraflores clifftop above the Costa Verde in Lima, near the hotel where BTS fans gathered (Photo: Avodrocc, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

MUSIC · PERU

Key Facts — The country Peru, where BTS, the South Korean pop group, is playing its first concerts: three nights at Estadio San Marcos in Lima on 7, 9 and 10 October.

— Why it matters The band’s leader, RM, publicly rebuked fans who crowded its hotel in Miraflores, the clifftop district where many foreign visitors to Lima stay.

— Why now The third and final Lima show is on Saturday 10 October. RM asked fans not to repeat the scenes in Chile, Brazil, Argentina or Asia.

— What happened On stage on Friday 9 October, RM said flying drones and pointing lasers at the hotel was “not a correct act”, after a fan drone show on Thursday 8 October.

— The numbers 150 drones were planned for the fan tribute. Police assigned 450 officers to the three concerts, and more than 180 buses run fans home.

— What it means for you Expect crowds near Larcomar and the Miraflores clifftop, and road closures around the stadium from 10 a.m. until 2 a.m. the next day.

— Still open Whether Barranco takes action against the drone organiser, and whether fans stay away from the hotel on the last night.

BTS, the South Korean pop group, has asked fans in Lima to stop gathering outside its hotel, before the last of its three concerts in Peru on Saturday 10 October. Its leader, RM, said on stage on Friday night that flying drones and pointing lasers at the building was wrong. The BTS Lima hotel crowds matter beyond Peru because RM said the same thing happens in Europe, Asia and the United States, and in an earlier Weverse message he asked fans to stay away from hotels for the rest of the tour.

The band is in Peru for the first time, on its World Tour ARIRANG. Its seven members are RM, Jin, SUGA, j-hope, Jimin, V and Jung Kook. The authorities expected tens of thousands of fans, mostly teenagers, at Estadio San Marcos in central Lima across the three shows, the state news agency Andina reported.

What RM Said on Stage

RM, whose real name is Kim Nam-joon, spoke near the end of the second concert on Friday 9 October, with the help of an interpreter. Lima broadcasters América TV and Panamericana both carried his words.

Latin America Power Index · October 2026 edition Peru ranks 5th of 14 with 54.7 points. Strongest pillar: military means (71); weakest: future resources (37). Alignment group: Closer to Washington. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

“The text I wrote was not only about Peru, or Latin America. It also happened in Europe, the United States; it can happen in Asia too, and it happens often,” he said. He added: “Flying drones or pointing lasers is really not a correct act.”

He also made clear the band holds no grudge against Peruvian fans. “When have we ever told people apart by nationality? Within ARMY and BTS, we are all the same people,” he said. ARMY is the name of the band’s fan community. He closed in Spanish: “Gracias, los amo Perú” (“Thank you, I love you, Peru”).

His remarks followed an earlier message on Weverse, the fan platform the band uses to talk to followers. In it, according to Infobae Peru, he wrote that “the members and the staff are having a very hard time” because of people outside the hotel all day. “The noise even reaches our rooms, so none of us is sleeping well,” he wrote, warning that a lack of rest would affect the shows.

How a Fan Tribute Turned Into a Crowd

The trigger was a drone show on the evening of Thursday 8 October over the Costa Verde, the seafront below the Miraflores and Barranco cliffs. Fans had promoted it as a welcome tribute, with 150 drones drawing the BTS logo and the members’ outlines in the sky, El Comercio reported.

After the show, crowds moved to the JW Marriott hotel next to the Larcomar shopping centre in Miraflores, where the band was reported to be staying. Videos shared on social media and described by Infobae Peru show people surrounding a black van as it tried to leave, while others shouted at them to “behave” and “let them through”. Infobae also reported that residents of Miraflores complained about the noise and traffic.

The Barranco district council said the event had no municipal permit. It said the organiser, a company named as Fanista Flit Perú, never applied for one. Peru’s civil aviation directorate at the Ministry of Transport had cleared the flights themselves, but the council said that did not replace its own permit for an event drawing a crowd. It added that the Barranco Tennis Club, the planned launch site, had been closed for lacking a valid building safety certificate.

Fans Turn on the Crowds

Peru’s organised fan groups have sided with the band. BTS Perú Fanclub, which helped promote the drone tribute, condemned what it called harassment outside the hotel. It said the show ran from 8:00 p.m. to 8:10 p.m. at a different site and never asked anyone to go to the hotel, Infobae reported.

Another account, ARMY Perú, shared on X a post attributed to a South Korean fan account, Eyop Korea, that described the scenes as a “serious invasion of privacy”, Infobae reported. Its claims of lasers aimed at hotel rooms have not been independently confirmed.

The concerts themselves have run in order. The national police assigned 450 officers to the stadium area for the three shows, and Lima’s transport authority laid on more than 180 buses for the journey home, the state news agency Andina said.

What It Means for You

For visitors in Lima on Saturday night, the main effects are traffic and crowds. Avenida Venezuela is closed near Estadio San Marcos from 10 a.m. until 2 a.m. the next morning on concert days, and the authorities advise against arriving by car. Around Larcomar, expect fans and police on the clifftop.

For fans following the tour from the United States or elsewhere, RM’s request applies to every stop. The band moves next to Chile, with three nights at Santiago’s Estadio Nacional, covered in BTS Chile Concerts Set for 14, 16 and 17 October. Ticket and entry details for Lima are in K-Pop Band BTS Plays 3 Sold-Out Shows in Lima Oct 2026.

The episode is also a reminder that the BTS Lima hotel scenes are a security question as much as a fan one. Lasers aimed at windows can damage eyesight, and crowds around moving vehicles carry obvious risks.

What Is Not Known

It is not known whether the hotel or the police have changed security arrangements for the final night. No arrests or formal complaints linked to the lasers have been reported. Reports differ on when RM posted his Weverse message; Panamericana dates it to Tuesday 6 October, Infobae to Wednesday 7 October, while his own words on stage suggest Thursday. Barranco has not said whether it will fine the drone organiser, and no one has said whether the BTS Lima hotel crowds will return on the final night.

Frequently Asked Questions

What did RM of BTS say about the hotel in Lima?

On stage on Friday 9 October, RM said flying drones or pointing lasers at the band’s hotel was not a correct act, and that crowding at hotels also happens in Europe, Asia and the United States.

Was the BTS drone show in Lima authorised?

The Ministry of Transport cleared the drone flights, but the Barranco district council said the organiser never applied for the municipal permit needed for an event that draws a crowd.

When is the last BTS concert in Lima?

The third and final Lima show is on Saturday 10 October 2026 at Estadio San Marcos. The band then plays Santiago, Chile, on 14, 16 and 17 October.

World.title: Djibouti Rises to Tier 2 in US Trafficking Report
World.content:
DJIBOUTI · HUMAN TRAFFICKING

Key Facts — What happened US State Department upgraded Djibouti to Tier 2 on 8 October.

— Two-year climb Tier 3 in 2024, Tier 2 Watch List in 2025.

— The numbers Six traffickers convicted, up from one; nine victims identified.

— The gaps No victims referred to care; national committee still has no chair.

— US link Djibouti hosts Camp Lemonnier, home of US forces in the Horn.

— Still open Djibouti’s government had not commented by Saturday, 10 October.

Two years after sitting on the bottom tier, Djibouti now shares Washington’s middle trafficking ranking with Ethiopia and Kenya.

The US State Department moved Djibouti up to Tier 2 in its 2026 Trafficking in Persons Report on Thursday, 8 October. The US trafficking report credits the Horn of Africa state with convicting more traffickers and identifying more victims.

It is Djibouti’s second upgrade in two years, after it sat on the lowest rung, Tier 3, in 2024. The ranking matters to Washington because Djibouti hosts Camp Lemonnier and overlooks the Bab el-Mandeb shipping lane.

The report still finds serious gaps, above all in care for victims. By Saturday, 10 October, no government statement had appeared on the state news agency ADI or in La Nation.

What the US Trafficking Report Says About Djibouti

The report says Djibouti “does not fully meet the minimum standards” against trafficking but “is making significant efforts to do so”. It found “overall increasing efforts compared with the previous reporting period; therefore, Djibouti was upgraded to Tier 2.”

The tiers come from the Trafficking Victims Protection Act, a US law passed in 2000. For governments on Tier 3, the US president decides whether to impose or waive limits on non-humanitarian, non-trade US aid.

The 2026 edition covers government action from 1 April 2025 to 31 March 2026. In the 2024 report, Djibouti “remained on Tier 3”; in 2025 it was “upgraded to Tier 2 Watch List”.

In the new rankings, Ethiopia and Kenya are also on Tier 2, while Eritrea sits on Tier 3. Somalia and Yemen, Djibouti’s neighbours by land and sea, are listed as special cases.

This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, Africa Intelligence. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

Six Convictions, but Victims Still Without State Care

Djibouti convicted six traffickers under its 2016 anti-trafficking law, up from one conviction a year earlier. Each received a two-year term, below the five to 10 years the law prescribes.

Officials credited expedited trial procedures introduced in 2024 for the rise. Investigations fell to three cases from six, while prosecutions rose to six defendants from five.

The government identified nine victims, up from five: five women, two men and two girls. Two were victims of forced labour; the form of trafficking was not specified for the other seven.

The report says the government again did not refer any victim to care. Shelter, health care and legal aid came from civil society groups “without any government funding or in-kind support”.

Djibouti also did not screen vulnerable groups, including Ethiopian migrants, for signs of trafficking. For the fourth year running, its anti-trafficking committee, created by presidential decree in 2023, had no chair.

There is still no national action plan and no money set aside for prevention, the report adds.

Labour Inspectors, New Courts and a Qatar Deal

On forced labour, the report notes progress. All 15 of Djibouti’s labour inspectors received anti-trafficking training, and three posts were designated to focus on trafficking.

The government also signed a new labour agreement with Qatar to protect migrant workers. A labour inspection procedure with anti-trafficking guidance was drafted but still awaited distribution.

The judiciary has begun efforts to set up courthouses in all five regions to cut case backlogs. A new courthouse in Dikhil, in the south-west, was finished but not yet operating.

On Thursday, 8 October, ADI reported on Labour Minister Yonis Ali Guedi’s talks in Dar es Salaam. At a labour mobility forum there, he met Qatar’s Labour Minister, Ali bin Samikh Al Marri.

The two ministers discussed new job openings for Djiboutian workers and “regular, transparent and protective” mobility.

On Friday, 9 October, ADI said Guedi had met Canada’s ambassador, Nicolas Simard, in Addis Ababa. A scheme sending Djiboutian heavy-truck drivers to Canada was called “an important first step”.

A Transit Hub on a Deadly Migrant Route

The report describes children from Ethiopia and Somalia forced to beg in Djibouti City. Women and children are exploited in domestic servitude and sex trafficking in Djibouti City, Ali Sabieh, Dikhil, Tadjourah and Obock.

Citing an international organisation, it says more than 290,000 Ethiopian migrants crossed Djibouti towards Saudi Arabia in the first half of 2025. Migrants leaving from Obock risk detention and ransom demands by criminal networks.

The UN migration agency, IOM, counted 922 deaths or disappearances on this “Eastern Route” in 2025, ADI reported on 7 October. Of 94 dead or missing in the first quarter of 2026, 61 were recorded in Djibouti.

IOM’s Djibouti chief, Alexandre Coissac, said more than 20,000 migrant movements from Ethiopia into Djibouti had been recorded since 10 September. In roughly the same weeks, more than 3,700 refugees fleeing fighting in Yemen landed on Djibouti’s coast.

Djibouti, a country of just over one million people, already hosts about 32,000 refugees and asylum seekers, the State Department says. Most come from Ethiopia, Somalia and Yemen.

What It Means for US Readers

Djibouti hosts Camp Lemonnier, home of the US military’s Combined Joint Task Force–Horn of Africa. Because only Tier 3 can trigger aid limits, the upgrade keeps that question off the table for now.

The report also flags at least 30 Cuban medical professionals working in Djibouti under a deal with Havana. It says the Cuban government may have forced them to work and that the deal leaves them exposed to wage confiscation.

For US firms using Djibouti’s ports and free zones, the report is a due-diligence signal. It names construction, domestic service and food service as sectors where foreign workers face forced labour.

The ranking changes no travel rules for Americans. It comes weeks after Djibouti signed the Artemis Accords, the US-led framework for civil space cooperation, according to the US Embassy.

What Is Not Known

Djibouti’s government had not commented on the upgrade by Saturday, 10 October. It is unclear whether it will now appoint a chair to its anti-trafficking committee or adopt an action plan.

The report does not name the six convicted traffickers or the courts that sentenced them. It also gives no date or terms for the new labour agreement with Qatar.

Whether the Dikhil courthouse has opened since 31 March, when the reporting period ended, is not stated.

What Comes Next

The next annual report will test whether Djibouti starts referring victims to care and funding prevention. Countries that fail to sustain progress can be moved down again.

The upgrade does not mean Djibouti meets US minimum standards; only Tier 1 countries do. In Africa, only Ghana reached Tier 1 this year.

Frequently Asked Questions

What Does Tier 2 Mean in the US Trafficking Report?

Tier 2 covers countries that do not fully meet US minimum standards against trafficking but are making significant efforts. Tier 1 countries fully meet those standards.

Why Was Djibouti Upgraded?

The State Department cited more prosecutions and convictions, more victims identified and new steps against forced labour. Those steps include training all labour inspectors and creating trafficking-focused posts.

What Problems Remain in Djibouti?

The government referred no victims to care and did not screen migrants for trafficking. Its anti-trafficking committee has had no chair for four years, and there is no action plan.

Why Does Djibouti Matter to the United States?

Djibouti hosts Camp Lemonnier, home of the US military’s task force for the Horn of Africa. It also overlooks the Bab el-Mandeb strait at the southern entrance to the Red Sea.

How Did Djibouti’s Neighbours Fare?

Ethiopia and Kenya are on Tier 2, and Eritrea is on Tier 3. Somalia and Yemen are listed as special cases.

World.title: Panama Declares State of Emergency After 7.7 Quake
World.content:
The Palacio de las Garzas in Panama City, seat of the presidency, where the Cabinet Council meets. (Photo: Ssaucedoc, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

DISASTER · PANAMA

Key Facts — The country Panama, a dollarised economy of about 4.5 million people, runs the canal. Its Tocumen airport is a key US link.

— Why it matters The emergency lets the government move money and staff fast to repair homes, schools and clinics hit by the quake.

— Why now More than 170 aftershocks kept shaking the country on Saturday, and damage reports kept growing in Coclé, Herrera, Los Santos and Veraguas.

— What happened The Cabinet Council approved a state of emergency on Saturday 10 October, after Friday’s magnitude 7.7 quake.

— The numbers Civil protection agency Sinaproc counts 27 injured, no deaths, more than 426 damaged homes and 21 damaged health facilities.

— What it means for you Travellers face pauses at Tocumen after each aftershock and no Metro service on Lines 1 and 2 on Saturday. US rescue teams are arriving.

— Still open The full cost of the damage, the size of the emergency budget and when schools and the Metro reopen.

Panama’s government declared a state of emergency on Saturday 10 October, a day after a magnitude 7.7 earthquake hit its Pacific side. The Panama state of emergency frees up money and staff for repairs to homes, schools and hospitals. For US travellers and companies, it signals that disruption at Panama’s airport, roads and public transport may last for days, not hours.

Juan Carlos Orillac, the minister of the presidency, announced the decision after President José Raúl Mulino met his cabinet on Saturday morning. Mulino, a conservative lawyer, has led Panama since July 2024.

“All ministers and institutions must be available and have the resources for solidarity aid to everyone affected,” Orillac said, according to La Estrella de Panamá. He said help would be organised as officials learn what each community needs.

Latin America Power Index · October 2026 edition Panama ranks 11th of 14 with 34.2 points. Strongest pillar: state capacity & security (64); weakest: military means (11). Alignment group: Closer to Washington. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

This is a follow-up to our earlier reports, Panama Hit by 7.7 Quake, Tsunami Alert Issued and US Mobilizes Help After 7.7 Panama Quake.

What the Emergency Declaration Does

The decree lets ministries and public bodies redirect funds and people to the disaster zone without the usual delays. Mulino ordered a three-person commission to steer the aid and the repair work.

Its members are Orillac, Canal Affairs Minister José Ramón Icaza and Vice Minister Virna Luque, La Estrella reported. La Prensa said the commission will also coordinate the reconstruction of damaged buildings.

The newspaper Panamá América and the news site Infobae reported that the emergency covers spending of up to US$100 million. Neither named an official source for the figure, and no decree had appeared in the Official Gazette by Saturday evening.

The government opened Parque Omar in Panama City as a collection centre for donations. Each provincial governor’s office will also receive aid. Consumer agency

This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, The LatAm Brief. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

Damage So Far

Malitzie Rivera, deputy director-general of Sinaproc, the national civil protection agency, gave the latest count at Saturday’s press conference. No deaths had been reported.

About 27 people were injured, with light to moderate wounds, and taken to hospitals. Sinaproc had inspected more than 426 homes with damage ranging from cracks to total collapse. Twenty-one health facilities were also hit.

Herrera, Los Santos and Veraguas have the most damaged homes. On Isla Cañas, off the Pacific coast, about 300 people were moved to safety after the sea rose. The Education Ministry counted 188 affected schools on Friday evening, a figure that may rise.

People injured in Panama's earthquake by province, Sinaproc preliminary report published Saturday 10 October; the Veraguas figure is one person rescued with injuries; no deaths reported. (Chart: Rio Times; data: Sinaproc via TVN)

The University of Panama’s Geosciences Institute puts the main shock at magnitude 7.5, northwest of Tonosí in Los Santos province. It struck at 12:56 p.m. on Friday (1:56 p.m. ET). The US Geological Survey measured it at 7.7.

The institute had recorded more than 170 aftershocks by Saturday afternoon, about seven an hour in the first 20 hours. Four were above magnitude 6: 6.9, 6.5, 6.2 and 6.1. It said aftershocks may continue for several weeks along a fault running about 230 kilometres west towards Coiba Island.

US Help on the Ground

A US military CH-47 Chinook from Joint Task Force-Bravo began flying tents and supplies to the Azuero peninsula on Saturday, TVN reported. Captain Daniel Betancourt, the US defence attaché in Panama, said three round trips were planned from Panamá Pacífico airport.

He also said at least 20 US search-and-rescue and structural-assessment specialists from Virginia and California were due to arrive.

What It Means for You

Tocumen International Airport, the hub of NYSE-listed Copa Airlines, stays open. However, it stops all take-offs and landings each time an aftershock is felt, then inspects runways before restarting. The airport warned this may cause new delays, so travellers should check with their airline.

In Panama City, Metro Lines 1 and 2 stayed shut on Saturday morning while engineers inspected the system. No restart time has been given.

Americans in Panama can follow US Embassy alerts and the State Department’s Smart Traveler programme. Investors should watch for a cost estimate, since the emergency spending will add to Panama’s public debt.

What Is Not Known

The government has not given a full damage bill or confirmed the budget behind the Panama state of emergency. It is also unclear how many families are homeless, as Sinaproc’s housing count is still rising.

Officials have not said when schools or the Metro will reopen. Damage counts from rural areas of Herrera, Los Santos and Veraguas are still coming in, so the toll may change.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why did Panama declare a state of emergency?

The Panama state of emergency was approved by the Cabinet Council on Saturday 10 October. It lets ministries move money and staff quickly to communities hit by Friday’s magnitude 7.7 earthquake.

How many people were hurt in the Panama earthquake?

Sinaproc, the civil protection agency, reported about 27 injured and no deaths by Saturday. It counted more than 426 damaged homes and 21 damaged health facilities.

Is it safe to fly to Panama after the earthquake?

Tocumen airport is operating, but it pauses flights after each felt aftershock to inspect runways. Delays are likely, so travellers should check flight status with their airline.

World.title: Brazil Canoe Champion With 2 Pan-Am Golds Dies in Rio
World.content:
The Quebra-Mar breakwater at the mouth of the Joatinga channel in Barra da Tijuca, Rio de Janeiro, seen from the air in 2017. (Photo: Diego Baravelli, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

SPORT · BRAZIL

Key Facts — The country Brazil. Rio de Janeiro’s Barra da Tijuca district has long beaches, lagoons and a breakwater, the Quebra-Mar, where the Joatinga channel meets the sea.

— Why it matters Rie Luciana Nagasako was a Pan-American champion in va’a, the Polynesian outrigger canoe best known in the United States from Hawaii.

— Why now She died on Friday 9 October, one day after falling into the sea while teaching a class near the Quebra-Mar.

— What happened On Thursday 8 October firefighters pulled her from the sea and flew her to Miguel Couto Municipal Hospital, where she died the next day.

— What it means for you Visitors who book canoe or paddle classes in Rio should check sea warnings, wear a well-fitted life jacket and ask instructors about their safety plan.

— Still open No official account of the cause has been published. Witness accounts of rough seas and a loosened life jacket remain unconfirmed.

A Brazil canoe champion, Rie Luciana Nagasako, died on Friday 9 October after falling into the sea during a class she was teaching in Rio de Janeiro.

She fell from an outrigger canoe on Thursday 8 October near the Quebra-Mar breakwater in Barra da Tijuca, in the city’s south-west zone.

For American and other foreign visitors, it is a reminder that Rio’s open-sea beaches can turn dangerous quickly, even for experts on calm-looking water.

Nagasako won two gold medals at the Pan-American va’a championship on Easter Island in November 2025, according to the Rio dailies O Globo and O Dia.

What Happened at the Quebra-Mar

Nagasako was leading a class when the accident happened on Thursday morning, according to G1, the news site of TV Globo.

G1 reported that she was trying to guide her students to turn their canoes towards a safer spot. During the manoeuvre she lost her balance and fell into the water.

The current carried her out, and the Rio de Janeiro state fire service, the Corpo de Bombeiros, rescued her offshore, G1 said.

Because of her condition, she was lifted out by air and taken to Miguel Couto Municipal Hospital in Gávea, in Rio’s south zone, in a very critical state.

G1 and O Dia reported that Rio’s Municipal Health Department confirmed her death on Friday afternoon. O Globo said the hospital’s management confirmed it.

G1 put the rescue at about 7 a.m., while O Globo said the fire service was called at 8:23 a.m. The fire service had not published its own timeline by Saturday evening.

What Witnesses Have Said

O Globo cited accounts posted by witnesses on social media. They said the sea was rough as Nagasako tried to bring a two-person canoe ashore at Praia dos Amores.

According to those accounts, the canoe lost control, was damaged and began to sink. Nagasako was steering from the rear seat.

The same posts said her life jacket loosened in the force of the water. The authorities have not confirmed these details.

Nagasako knew the area well. In a 2025 interview with O Globo, she warned that silt at the mouth of the Joatinga channel made passage harder for canoes.

She also called for closer checks on motorboats around the beaches and lagoons, the paper said.

Who Was Rie Luciana Nagasako

Nagasako was a competitor and a coach. G1 and O Dia said she founded the Barra Va’a club and a community programme called Projeto Somar.

Va’a is the Tahitian name for the outrigger canoe. Crews of one, two, three or six paddlers race on the open sea, and the sport has a large following in Hawaii and Brazil.

At the Pan-American championship on Easter Island, a Chilean territory in the Pacific, she won the V6 Master and V3 Open events, O Globo and O Dia reported.

V6 Master is a six-paddler event for crews aged over 40. V3 Open is raced in three-seat canoes with no age limit.

G1, O Globo and O Dia said she had also won a bronze medal in the sprint category at the sport’s world championship.

O Globo said her competitive career began only in 2022. Without a sponsor, she raised money on social media to represent Brazil at the Pan-American event.

Her death prompted a wave of tributes from students and paddlers. The Brazilian Va’a Confederation mourned her, and on Saturday morning friends and family gathered at Praia dos Amores, where she taught, O Dia reported.

What It Means for You

Outrigger canoe and stand-up paddle classes are offered on several Rio beaches, and many visitors book them. Most outings end without incident, and instructors usually stay close to shore.

The death of a Brazil canoe champion in familiar waters shows that conditions near breakwaters and channel mouths can change within minutes.

Before going out, check the Brazilian Navy’s weather and swell warnings, which flag the strong swells Brazilians call ressaca. Ask the instructor how they will respond if someone falls in.

Make sure your life jacket is your size and fastened tightly. In an emergency, Brazil’s fire service answers on 193, and lifeguard posts line Barra’s beachfront.

For the day’s other news from the city, see our Rio de Janeiro Daily Brief for Saturday, October 10, 2026. For road safety this holiday weekend, read Brazil Highway Crash Kills 5 From One Family on BR-393.

What Is Not Known

No authority has published an official account of how the accident happened or what caused the canoe to fail.

It is not known whether the Brazilian Navy’s port authority, which oversees safety at sea, or the police have opened an inquiry.

The sea conditions on Thursday morning, the state of the canoe and the fit of Nagasako’s life jacket have not been confirmed. Her family has started an online fundraiser for the wake and cremation, for which no date or place had been set on Saturday, O Dia reported.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who was the Brazil canoe champion who died in Rio?

Rie Luciana Nagasako, a paddler and coach who founded the Barra Va’a club. She won two golds at the Pan-American va’a championship on Easter Island in November 2025.

How did Rie Luciana Nagasako die?

She fell into the sea on Thursday 8 October while teaching a class near the Quebra-Mar in Barra da Tijuca. Firefighters rescued her and she died in hospital on Friday 9 October.

Is it safe to take a canoe class in Rio de Janeiro?

Most classes pass without incident. Check Navy swell warnings, wear a life jacket that fits tightly, and ask the instructor about their safety plan before going out.

Sources: Rio Municipal Health Department and Miguel Couto hospital statements as reported by G1, O Globo and O Dia; Correio; Agenda do Poder; Brasil em Folhas.

World.title: José Sarney, 96, Enters Intensive Care After Surgery
World.content:
President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva greets former president José Sarney at the Sarney family residence in São Luís, Maranhão, on 21 June 2024. (Photo: Ricardo Stuckert/PR, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

POLITICS · BRAZIL

Key Facts — The country Brazil is Latin America’s largest economy and a major US trade partner. Its former president Sarney, 96, led the country from 1985 to 1990.

— Why it matters Sarney led the 1985 handover from military rule to civilian government. His health is followed closely across Brazil’s political class.

— Why now It is his third hospital stay in about a month, after two admissions for bacterial pneumonia in September.

— What happened On Friday 9 October Sarney was admitted with abdominal pain in São Luís and had surgery to clear an intestinal obstruction. He is in intensive care.

— What it means for you There is no market or travel impact. For readers following Brazil’s 25 October runoff, it is a human story, not a policy one.

— Still open The hospital has given no discharge date. It has not said how long he will stay in intensive care or what caused the obstruction.

Former Brazilian president José Sarney, 96, is in intensive care in São Luís after abdominal surgery on Friday 9 October.

The hospital says the operation went without complications and that he is stable, awake and under the care of a multidisciplinary team.

For American readers, he is the man who steered Brazil from military rule to democracy in 1985, and who met Ronald Reagan at the White House as president.

Latin America Power Index · October 2026 edition Brazil ranks 1st of 14 with 75.0 points. Strongest pillar: military means (100); weakest: state capacity & security (56). Alignment group: Hedging. WatchRating below investment grade (BB); public debt at 93% of GDP. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

His admission comes two weeks before Brazil’s presidential runoff on Sunday 25 October, and barely a month after he was treated for pneumonia.

What the Hospital Says

Sarney was admitted to UDI Hospital in São Luís, the capital of the northeastern state of Maranhão, on Friday afternoon. The private hospital is run by Rede D’Or, one of Brazil’s largest hospital groups.

According to the medical bulletin quoted by Agência Brasil, the federal public news agency, he arrived with abdominal pain. Doctors carried out a clinical assessment and imaging tests before operating.

“At the moment, the patient is stable, in post-operative monitoring in the intensive care unit, where he remains under the care of a multidisciplinary team,” the bulletin said. It gave no discharge date.

G1 and the São Luís news site Imirante described the operation as surgery to clear an intestinal obstruction. Estadão reported that the hospital note was signed by its medical director, Dr Julia Bacelar Barros.

A newer bulletin released on Saturday 10 October, as reported by G1 and Imirante, said Sarney was awake and haemodynamically stable. That means his circulation and heart function were steady.

He remains under the joint care of the intensive care and digestive surgery teams, G1 said. There is still no forecast for discharge.

A Third Hospital Stay in About a Month

The latest admission follows two spells in hospital in September for bacterial pneumonia. The illness was first diagnosed and treated at the same UDI Hospital in São Luís, where he spent three days, from 13 to 16 September, G1 reported. The Rio Times covered that stay in José Sarney Became Brazil’s President Because Another Man Died. He Is in Hospital at 96.

On 24 September he flew to São Paulo for a check-up at Hospital Sírio-Libanês, one of the country’s best-known private hospitals, and was admitted again. Doctors there were coordinated by cardiologist Roberto Kalil Filho, G1 reported.

He left that hospital around the turn of the month, only days before the first round of voting.

On Sunday 4 October, Sarney voted in São Luís, accompanied by his grandson Adriano Sarney. “I am very moved and, at the same time, very pleased when I see the democratic celebration Brazil is living,” he told reporters, according to G1.

His daughter Roseana Sarney, also of the MDB, ran for the Senate in that election. Estadão reported that she finished third and lost.

Who Sarney Is

Sarney was the first president of Brazil’s return to civilian rule, serving from 1985 to 1990, Agência Brasil notes. He then served three terms in the Senate, from 1991 to 2015.

Folha de S.Paulo lists him as a member of the MDB, the Brazilian Democratic Movement, a large centrist party.

Agência Brasil describes him as a writer as well as a politician. His family remains active in Maranhão politics.

What It Means for You

For investors, there is no market story here. Sarney holds no office, and his health has no direct bearing on Brazilian assets or the real.

For travellers, nothing in the hospital bulletins affects visits to São Luís or the rest of Maranhão.

For readers following Brazilian politics, Sarney is a link to the generation that rebuilt democracy after 1985. The country heads into a polarised runoff with both camps busy campaigning. Our latest poll coverage is in Brazil Runoff Poll Gives Bolsonaro Son 52%, Lula 48%.

The calmer reading is that the surgery went without complications and that he is awake and stable. The risk is his age and the recent pneumonia, which make any recovery slower.

What Is Not Known

The hospital has not said what caused the intestinal obstruction or how long he will need intensive care.

No discharge date has been given. It is also not known whether doctors plan any further procedures.

It is unclear when the next medical bulletin will be published. The Rio Times will rely only on official hospital statements.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why is Sarney in intensive care?

He was admitted on Friday 9 October with abdominal pain and had surgery to clear an intestinal obstruction. The hospital says he is stable and recovering in the intensive care unit.

Where is José Sarney being treated?

At UDI Hospital in São Luís, the capital of Maranhão state. The private hospital belongs to Rede D’Or, one of Brazil’s largest hospital groups.

Who is José Sarney?

He was Brazil’s president from 1985 to 1990, the first of the return to civilian rule. He later served three Senate terms, from 1991 to 2015, and is also a writer.

Sources: UDI Hospital (Rede D’Or) medical bulletins as reported by Agência Brasil; G1 Maranhão (9 October); G1 Maranhão (10 October); Folha de S.Paulo; Estadão; Imirante.

World.title: Honduras Inflation Climbs to 6.28% on Fuel and Food
World.content:
A roadside fruit stall in Sabá, Colón, Honduras. Food added 1.57 points to September inflation (Photo: kristin klein, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

ECONOMY · HONDURAS

Key Facts — The country Honduras, a Central American economy of about 10 million people that imports its fuel and relies heavily on money sent home by workers abroad.

— Why it matters Inflation is now above the central bank’s 4% target range and above its 6% policy rate, squeezing households that live on remittances from the United States.

— Why now The Banco Central de Honduras published its September price report on Saturday 10 October.

— What happened Annual inflation rose to 6.28% in September from 6.20% in August and 4.55% a year earlier. Monthly inflation slowed to 0.48% from 0.79%.

— The numbers Transport prices are up 16.05% on the year and added 2.67 points. Food added 1.57 points. Core inflation was 3.47%.

— What it means for you Dollars sent to Honduras buy less food and transport than a year ago. Travellers and investors face higher local costs, led by fuel.

— Still open Whether the central bank raises its policy rate again after September’s hike, and whether world oil prices ease before the dry season.

Honduras inflation rose to 6.28% in September, the highest annual rate in the past year of official data. The Banco Central de Honduras (BCH), the country’s central bank, published the figure on Saturday 10 October. For Americans, the number matters because millions of Hondurans live on dollars sent from the United States, and those dollars now stretch less far.

The bank blamed imported fuel and the weather. Higher world oil prices, linked to tensions in the Middle East, raised transport and logistics costs. The El Niño weather pattern pushed up prices of dairy, sugar, beef and red beans.

There is a stabiliser in the same report. Prices rose 0.48% in September alone, down from 0.79% in August. Core inflation, which strips out the most volatile items, was 3.47%, inside the bank’s target band.

Fuel and Food Drive the Rise

Transport is the largest single driver. Its prices are 16.05% higher than a year ago, and the division added 2.67 percentage points to the annual rate, according to the BCH tables.

Food and non-alcoholic drinks rose 6.01% on the year and added 1.57 points. The bank named fizzy drinks, potatoes, eggs and chicken among the items that weighed most.

Housing, water, electricity and gas added 0.74 points. Restaurants and hotels added 0.52 points, as eateries passed on higher costs for food and cooking fuel.

Looked at another way, energy alone contributed 2.40 points. The bank linked this to higher international oil prices and to consecutive increases in the electricity tariff over the past year.

Annual inflation in Honduras climbed from 4.55% a year ago to 6.28% in September, above the 4% target band. In September itself, the items with the biggest price rises included diesel, super and regular petrol, eggs, onions, maize and beans. Prices fell for potatoes, airfares, avocados, butter, beds, refrigerators and motorcycles. The bank said cheaper flights reflected the low travel season.

The rise was broad but narrowing. Of the 405 goods and services in the basket, 59.5% rose in price in September, down from 64.0% in August.

This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, The LatAm Brief. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

Where Prices Rose Fastest

The southern region, which borders El Salvador and Nicaragua on the Gulf of Fonseca, had the highest annual rate at 7.49%. It was also the only region where inflation slowed, from 7.79% in August.

The rest of the north stood at 6.77% and the rest of the central region at 6.71%. The capital district of Tegucigalpa recorded 6.07%. Metropolitan San Pedro Sula, the country’s main industrial city, recorded 5.94%.

The year so far tells a similar story. Prices are up 5.29% since December, against 4.00% at the same point in 2025. The trough came in February, when the annual rate fell to 3.46%.

The BCH sets a target of 4% with a tolerance of one point either side. Headline Honduras inflation has been above that band since April. On Friday 18 September the bank raised its policy rate by a quarter point to 6.00% from 5.75%, effective 21 September, citing fuel prices and a US Federal Reserve hike. That rate is now slightly below annual inflation.

Fuel has also been a political issue under President Nasry Asfura, of the conservative National Party, who took office in January. Background on the government’s price steps is in Honduras Freezes Diesel at US$5.72 for 30 Days and Honduras Energy Justice Law in Force, Tariffs Frozen.

What It Means for You

If you send money to family in Honduras, each dollar buys less food and transport than a year ago. Remittances have still grown fast. BCH data show US$8.92 billion arrived from January to August, up about 12% from US$7.94 billion a year earlier.

For travellers, the biggest increases are in fuel, buses and restaurant meals. Airfares within the index fell in September. The central bank’s reference rate was 26.89 lempiras per US dollar on Wednesday 7 October.

For investors and exporters, higher fuel and logistics costs raise operating costs in the maquila factories and farms that supply the US market. September’s rate hike already makes local borrowing dearer, and the bank has not said whether more will follow.

What Is Not Known

It is not known whether the BCH will raise its 6% policy rate again after the September hike. The September report describes prices but does not set out a policy decision.

It is unclear how long fuel relief measures will last, or how world oil prices will move. The bank says Honduras depends heavily on imported fuel, so any shock abroad reaches pump prices quickly.

The weather is another unknown. Heavy rains have hit parts of the country this month, and the bank warns that climate effects keep pushing up farm prices. The October figure is due in November.

Frequently Asked Questions

What was Honduras inflation in September 2026?

Annual consumer price inflation was 6.28% in September 2026, up from 6.20% in August and 4.55% in September 2025, according to the Banco Central de Honduras.

Why are prices rising in Honduras?

The central bank points to higher world oil prices, which lift transport and logistics costs, and to El Niño weather effects on farm products such as dairy, sugar, beef and beans.

What is the central bank’s inflation target?

The target is 4% with a tolerance of one percentage point either side. Core inflation, at 3.47%, is inside that band, while headline inflation is above it.

Sources: Banco Central de Honduras, Índice de Precios al Consumidor, September 2026 report; Banco Central de Honduras, consumer price index page and indicators (inflation, policy rate, remittances, exchange rate); Banco Central de Honduras, Resolution No. 393-9/2026 on the policy rate; HCH, “Inflación en Honduras alcanza 6.28% en septiembre por alza de combustibles y factores climáticos”, 10 October 2026.
