World.title: Paraguay Trafficking Probes Halve as US Keeps Tier 2
World.content:
A ship docked on the Paraguay River at dusk. The US State Department report describes sex trafficking on river vessels in Paraguay. (Photo: Cmasi, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

HUMAN RIGHTS · PARAGUAY

Key Facts — The country Paraguay, a landlocked South American farm exporter between Argentina, Brazil and Bolivia, and a close US security partner.

— Why it matters The US grade shapes aid decisions and flags forced-labour risk in supply chains that reach American buyers.

— Why now The State Department released its 2026 Trafficking in Persons Report on Thursday 8 October. Paraguay’s press picked up its chapter on Friday 9 October.

— What happened Paraguay stayed on Tier 2. Investigations fell to 69 in 2025 from 139 in 2024.

— The numbers Convictions rose to 16 from 4, prosecutions to 50 suspects from 12, identified victims to 221 from 104.

— What it means for you US importers sourcing Paraguayan farm goods should note the report’s forced-labour findings in agriculture.

— Still open Why investigations halved, and whether the government will fund its anti-trafficking programme as the law requires.

Paraguay trafficking investigations fell by half last year, even as convictions quadrupled, the US State Department says in its new annual report. Washington kept the South American country on Tier 2, the middle grade. For US readers, the grade matters because it shapes aid decisions and flags forced-labour risk in farm supply chains.

The 2026 Trafficking in Persons Report was released on Thursday 8 October. Its Paraguay trafficking chapter says the government “does not fully meet the minimum standards for the elimination of trafficking” but is making significant efforts.

Asunción daily Última Hora reported the findings on Friday 9 October. It highlighted the Paraguay trafficking gaps the report lists in shelter, funding and child domestic labour.

Latin America Power Index · October 2026 edition Paraguay ranks 10th of 14 with 36.0 points. Strongest pillar: state capacity & security (55); weakest: future resources (13). Alignment group: Closer to Washington. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

What the US Report Says About Paraguay

The State Department grades every government each year under the Trafficking Victims Protection Act of 2000. Tier 1 is for countries that fully meet its minimum standards. Tier 3 is for those that do not and are not making significant efforts.

Paraguay sits in between. The report credits “overall increasing efforts” compared with the previous year, which is why the grade held.

It lists the gains. Authorities prosecuted and convicted more traffickers and identified more victims. Agencies coordinated better on victim care, and the government updated procedures to help Paraguayans exploited abroad.

It also lists the failures. Investigations fell, officials screened vulnerable groups inconsistently, and adult male victims had no shelter. The national anti-trafficking programme was underfunded and still lacked the dedicated funding stream that the law requires.

Paraguay’s 2012 anti-trafficking law, Law 4788, sets prison terms of up to eight years for sex and labour trafficking involving adults, the report says. Cases involving children carry two to 20 years.

The State Department has a technical objection to that law. It treats force, fraud and coercion as aggravating factors rather than core elements of the crime. The report calls this inconsistent with the international definition.

Follow this story Get an email when there’s news on Paraguay Email address Follow Free. One email a day at most, and only when there is news. This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, The LatAm Brief. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

Fewer Cases, More Convictions

Authorities opened 69 Paraguay trafficking investigations in 2025, down from 139 in 2024. Of the new cases, 24 concerned sex trafficking, 32 forced labour and 13 were unspecified.

Prosecutions moved the other way. Prosecutors charged 50 suspects, up from 12 the year before. Courts convicted 16 traffickers, up from four, of whom 13 were convicted of sex trafficking and three of forced labour.

Paraguay opened fewer trafficking investigations in 2025 but prosecuted and convicted more suspects. (Chart: Rio Times; data: US State Department, 2026 Trafficking in Persons Report)

The government did not report sentences. It reported no investigations, prosecutions or convictions of officials for complicity, and cited a lack of resources and capacity.

Victim identification more than doubled. The report counts 221 victims in 2025, against 104 in 2024. Of those, 51 were sex trafficking victims, 108 labour trafficking victims and 62 unspecified. The government assisted 90 of them.

Support remained thin. Victims had to be formally certified before they could get health care, legal help or repatriation. The government reported no residence permits for foreign victims, and no victims chose to take part in criminal proceedings.

Criadazgo and Recruitment Online

The report singles out criadazgo. Under this custom, poor rural families send children to live with wealthier households, where they work in exchange for board and schooling. The report says it can lead to trafficking.

Paraguay’s Senate rejected a bill to criminalise the practice in May 2025. Última Hora reported that senators Gustavo Leite and Dionisio Amarilla defended criadazgo during the debate as part of Paraguayan culture. Nobody knows how many children live in it today, the paper said.

Recruitment has moved online. Traffickers use social media to post deceptive job offers, the report says, or threaten to share intimate images. Paraguayan victims have been found in Argentina, Brazil, Cambodia and Europe.

Inside the country, the report describes sex trafficking aboard river vessels, and says child sex trafficking cases often involve a family member. It documents forced labour in agriculture and aquaculture. Children in street vending, begging, mining, brick making and ranching are vulnerable, and traffickers force children to grow and sell illicit drugs. Indigenous and rural Paraguayans are the most exposed.

The grade puts Paraguay alongside the Dominican Republic, covered in Dominican Republic Stays Tier 2 on US Trafficking List. Its neighbour fared worse, as reported in Brazil Stays on US Trafficking Watch List on 8 October.

What It Means for You

For US companies, the forced-labour findings are the practical point. Section 307 of the US Tariff Act bars imports made with forced labour. Buyers of Paraguayan farm and fish products may face more due-diligence questions.

For policy watchers, Tier 2 keeps Paraguay clear of the aid restrictions that can follow a Tier 3 grade. President Santiago Peña, in office since August 2023, leads one of Washington’s closest partners in South America.

For travellers and families, the report is a reminder about online job offers abroad. It names social media as the main recruiting channel. The stabiliser: Paraguay runs an anti-trafficking hotline and regulates labour recruiters, the report says.

The Cambodia mention stands out. Washington has sanctioned operators of Southeast Asian scam compounds that use trafficked workers. The report does not say what work the Paraguayan victims there were forced to do.

What Is Not Known

The report does not explain why Paraguay trafficking investigations halved while prosecutions rose. It does not give budget figures, only that resources were insufficient.

Paraguay’s government had not publicly responded to the chapter by Saturday 10 October, as far as Rio Times could find. It is also unclear whether lawmakers will revisit criadazgo before the extended national action plan runs out in 2026.

Frequently Asked Questions

What tier is Paraguay in the 2026 US trafficking report?

Paraguay is on Tier 2. The State Department says it does not fully meet the minimum standards to eliminate trafficking but is making significant efforts, which increased compared with the previous year.

How many trafficking cases did Paraguay investigate in 2025?

Authorities opened 69 investigations in 2025, down from 139 in 2024. They prosecuted 50 suspects and convicted 16 traffickers, against 12 and four the year before.

What is criadazgo in Paraguay?

Criadazgo is a custom in which children from poor families live and work in other households in exchange for board and schooling. The US report says it can lead to trafficking. The Senate rejected a bill to ban it in May 2025.

Sources: US Department of State, 2026 Trafficking in Persons Report: Paraguay; Última Hora, EEUU advierte que Paraguay no cumple estándares para erradicar la trata de personas.

World.title: Bolivia Keeps Petrol Subsidy Until January Review
World.content:
Traffic and street trade in the Ballivián area of El Alto. Petrol stays subsidised in Bolivia for the rest of 2026, the economy minister said. (Photo: Chavezrodri1, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons)

ECONOMY · BOLIVIA

Key Facts — The country Bolivia, a landlocked Andean nation of about 11 million people, short of dollars and fuel, now under a 36-month IMF programme.

— Why it matters Fuel subsidies are the most sensitive part of the IMF deal. The diesel subsidy has already gone; petrol, power and gas reach nearly every household.

— Why now Reports this week said the IMF plan aligns pump prices with world prices in early 2027, raising fears of wider cuts.

— What happened On Friday 9 October, Economy Minister Christian Morales said the IMF deal covers only motor fuels, not electricity or gas, and petrol stays subsidised in 2026.

— The numbers Subsidised petrol costs about US$2.25 a gallon, against a US average of US$4.37 (AAA, 10 October).

— What it means for you Visitors and residents keep cheap petrol and current power and gas tariffs for now; the next decision point is a review in January.

— Still open How fast petrol prices rise in 2027, and how much cash support poorer households and transport operators will get.

Bolivia will remove its fuel subsidy only for motor fuels and will not touch electricity or gas under its deal with the International Monetary Fund (IMF), Economy Minister Christian Morales said on Friday 9 October. He also ruled out lifting the Bolivia fuel subsidy on petrol (gasoline) for the rest of 2026. For US investors holding Bolivian bonds, the message is that the IMF programme stands, while the government tries to limit street protests.

Morales, who runs the Ministry of Economy and Public Finance under President Rodrigo Paz, spoke on the Red Uno programme Que No Me Pierda. He was asked directly whether power and gas subsidies could follow petrol and diesel.

“No. It is an issue that is not contemplated in the agreement; it is not an issue we will move on during the next administrative year,” he said, according to Red Uno. The outlet eju.tv reported the same remarks on Saturday.

Latin America Power Index · October 2026 edition Bolivia ranks 12th of 14 with 28.4 points. Strongest pillar: military means (55); weakest: diplomatic & cultural influence (13). Alignment group: Hedging. WatchRating below investment grade (CCC+); economy contracting (-1.2%); inflation of 20%. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

What the Minister Said

Morales confirmed that the IMF agreement foresees the full removal of subsidies on motor fuels. “The agreement with the Monetary Fund establishes the lifting of the complete fuel subsidy,” he said.

He said the process began early with diesel, whose subsidy has already gone. Petrol is part of the deal too, but its timing depends on the economy, public finances and world oil prices.

“In this current year we do not plan to lift the gasoline subsidy,” Morales said. He added that a decree in force sets an evaluation date in January 2027, but he would not say that prices will rise on that day. “What is appropriate is precisely to carry out an evaluation on that date,” he said.

On electricity, Morales said the government is working on a change in the country’s energy mix to cut what it spends on power generation. He described this as a separate policy, not part of the IMF deal.

The IMF Executive Board approved Bolivia’s 36-month Extended Fund Facility arrangement on Friday 2 October, according to the Fund. According to eju.tv, the IMF foresees full alignment of retail fuel prices with international prices in early 2027. Our earlier report, Bolivia IMF Deal Sets Path to World Fuel Prices, covered that plan.

How Cheap Bolivian Fuel Is

The government raised petrol to Bs 6.96 a litre (about US$0.59) in December 2025, according to eju.tv. That is roughly US$2.25 a gallon at the central bank’s official rate of 11.73 bolivianos per US dollar, valid for 10 to 12 October.

The AAA national average for regular petrol in the United States was US$4.37 a gallon on 10 October. The comparison is not exact, because US prices include taxes, but it shows the size of the gap the subsidy covers.

Subsidised Bolivian petrol costs about half the US average. Bolivian price of 6.96 bolivianos a litre converted at the Banco Central de Bolivia official rate of 11.73 per US dollar. Diesel is already sold without a subsidy, the minister said. The earlier diesel step and its effect on queues are covered in Bolivia Diesel Subsidy Ends: Price Rises 83% as Fuel Queues Shrink.

What It Means for You

For travellers and foreign residents, the practical change is small for now. Petrol prices should stay where they are until at least the January review, and household power and gas bills are not part of the IMF deal.

For investors, the statement narrows the political risk. A cut to electricity or cooking gas would hit almost every household at once. Limiting the reform to motor fuels makes the programme easier to defend, though the petrol step in 2027 remains the hardest one.

The government says it will protect poorer groups. Morales cited cash transfers, including the PEPE bonus paid after the diesel increase, according to Red Uno. He also mentioned a trust fund of Bs 800 million (about US$68 million) to help producers and transport operators get credit.

“We are not going to leave the most vulnerable sectors aside,” he said. The government plans talks with economic groups in the coming months to decide how to handle petrol in 2027.

What Is Not Known

We could not open the IMF programme document itself. The early-2027 price target rests on Bolivian media reports of its contents, and the minister’s account of what it excludes has not been published by the Fund.

It is not known how large the first petrol increase will be, or whether it will come in one step or several. Morales said world prices and public finances could change the plan, and that some decisions may need to be reviewed with the IMF.

The size and timing of any new cash transfers for 2027 have not been set. The minister gave no figure for how much the petrol subsidy costs the state each year.

The Bolivia fuel subsidy debate will return before January. For now, the government has drawn a clear line: motor fuels change, power and gas do not.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is Bolivia removing subsidies on electricity and gas?

No. Economy Minister Christian Morales said on 9 October that the IMF agreement does not include power or gas subsidies, and that the government will not move on them next year.

When will petrol prices rise in Bolivia?

Not in 2026, according to the minister. A decree sets an evaluation in January 2027, but he did not commit to a price rise on that date.

How much does petrol cost in Bolivia?

The subsidised price is about US$0.59 a litre, or roughly US$2.25 a gallon, compared with a US average of about US$4.37 a gallon on 10 October.

World.title: Chon Saan opens in San Pedro today, bringing its famous Chinese cuisine to Ambergris Caye
World.content:
Chon Saan opens in San Pedro today, bringing its famous Chinese cuisine to Ambergris Caye

By Breaking Belize News Staff: One of Belize’s most recognizable restaurant brands is expanding to Ambergris Caye as Chon Saan Palace officially opens its doors in San Pedro today, Saturday, October 10, at noon.

Restaurant owner and Mesopotamia Area Representative Lee Mark Chang confirmed the opening to Breaking Belize News (BBN) this morning, sharing photos of the final preparations at the new establishment.

The restaurant, located on Middle Street in downtown San Pedro, diagonally across from Elvi’s Kitchen, occupies the ground floor of the Sun & Reef Hotel, where a casino previously operated.

Chang said the restaurant will initially accommodate approximately 48 diners, with nine tables available. However, plans are already being considered to expand operations onto the building’s second floor.

The restaurant will operate from 11 a.m. to 3 p.m. and reopen from 5 p.m. to 10 p.m., with Tuesdays designated as its weekly day off.

Chang also indicated that Chon Saan remains open to recruiting talented individuals as the business expands.

The San Pedro location will feature many of the dishes that have made Chon Saan a household name in Belize, including its popular fried chicken, Chinese specialties, noodles, soups and other favourites. The restaurant will initially offer dine-in and takeout services, with delivery services planned for a later stage.

Chon Saan’s history dates back to 1974, when Chang’s parents, Armando Chang and his wife, established the original family restaurant on Douglas Jones Street in Belize City. Over the decades, the business grew into one of the country’s best-known Chinese restaurants, celebrating its 50th anniversary in 2024.

The opening marks another chapter in the restaurant’s more than five decades of operations, bringing its longstanding culinary tradition to residents and visitors of Belize’s leading tourism destination.

World.title: Chebat meets BDF top brass at Senior Officers’ Conference
World.content:
Chebat meets BDF top brass at Senior Officers’ Conference

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Newly appointed Minister of National Security Michel Chebat has met with the senior leadership of the Belize Defence Force.

The meeting took place on Friday, October 9, at the BDF’s annual Senior Officers’ Conference, held at the Biltmore Plaza Hotel in Belize City.

Chebat introduced himself to the Force’s senior officers, engaged with the leadership and shared his strategic guidance and vision for the way forward.

Also in attendance were Major (Retired) Francis Usher, Chief Executive Officer of the Ministry of National Security, BDF Commander Brigadier General Anthony Velasquez, senior BDF officers and high ranking foreign military partners.

The conference comes just days after Chebat took on the expanded National Security portfolio, which now places both the BDF and the Belize Police Department under his ministry.

World.title: BTV spots Guatemalan military boat near Sarstoon Island amid ongoing tensions
World.content:
BTV spots Guatemalan military boat near Sarstoon Island amid ongoing tensions

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Belize Territorial Volunteers (BTV) leader Wil Maheia is reporting another sighting of a Guatemalan Armed Forces (GAF) vessel near Sarstoon Island, as tensions continue along Belize’s southern border.

Maheia, who was travelling in the Sarstoon area early Saturday morning, shared video footage with Breaking Belize News showing the river and vessels in the distance. He reported spotting a Guatemalan military boat near Sarstoon Island, an area that has been at the centre of repeated confrontations between Belizean civilians and Guatemalan security forces.

The latest sighting comes exactly one month after a major confrontation on September 10, when the BTV was prevented from completing its traditional journey around Sarstoon Island. According to Belize’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs, approximately 18 Guatemalan military and civilian vessels were deployed near the island, prompting Belizean security forces to limit the expedition to the Belize Defence Force’s Forward Operating Base.

The Government of Belize subsequently lodged a formal diplomatic protest, accusing Guatemala of violating Belize’s sovereignty and obstructing the lawful passage of unarmed Belizean nationals. Belize maintains that the international boundary follows the mid-channel of the Sarstoon River under the 1859 Boundary Treaty and that Sarstoon Island falls entirely within Belizean territory.

Tensions were further heightened on September 24 when a Guatemalan military reconnaissance aircraft entered Belizean airspace without authorization. The National Security Council subsequently directed the Government to request an investigation by the Organization of American States, citing repeated incursions by Guatemalan forces into Belize’s southern maritime territory and threats involving the Sarstoon.

Both countries remain engaged in proceedings before the International Court of Justice (ICJ), which is expected to hear oral arguments in February 2027 concerning Guatemala’s longstanding territorial, insular and maritime claim against Belize.

Saturday’s reported sighting underscores the continued sensitivity of the Sarstoon area as Belize and Guatemala await a final resolution to their territorial dispute.

World.title: Tensions continue at the Sarstoon
World.content:
Tensions continue at the Sarstoon

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): The Sarstoon is once again in the spotlight.

On Saturday morning, Belize Territorial Volunteers leader Wil Maheia reported seeing a Guatemalan Armed Forces vessel in Belizean waters in front of Sarstoon Island during an early morning trip to the area.

The sighting comes amid rising tensions between Belize and Guatemala.

On September 10, the Guatemalan Navy made an incursion into the Sarstoon. Then, on September 24, a Guatemalan military reconnaissance aircraft entered Belizean airspace, an incursion the National Security Council confirmed this week using radar data.

In response, Government has asked the Organization of American States to investigate the airspace incident and has called on Guatemala to respect long established confidence building measures.

Government has also pointed to multiple incursions by the Guatemalan Armed Forces into Belize’s southern maritime space and threats of the use of force on the Sarstoon in recent months.

Newly appointed Minister of National Security Michel Chebat has pledged to strengthen Belize’s security cooperation and protect the country’s sovereignty.

There has been no official response yet to Saturday’s sighting.

World.title: Jarred Gongora charged with aggravated assault and firearm offenses following incident involving Kevin Trapp in Unitedville
World.content:
Jarred Gongora charged with aggravated assault and firearm offenses following incident involving Kevin Trapp in Unitedville

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Police have formally arrested and charged 38-year-old Jarred Denver Gongora, a Belizean laborer from the Cayo District, following an incident involving Kevin Trapp in Unitedville Village.

According to police, the incident occurred on Thursday, October 8, in the Spanishtown area of Unitedville. Gongora was arrested on Friday, October 9, and charged with aggravated assault, keeping a firearm without a gun license, and keeping ammunition without a gun license.

Trapp has previously been the target of gun violence. In November 2025, he survived an ambush near the Unitedville Community Centre when a gunman opened fire as he arrived home in his vehicle. He sustained multiple gunshot wounds and was hospitalized.

In June 2026, Trapp was also among five people jointly charged with firearm and ammunition offenses after police discovered a loaded .22-calibre pistol during a Special Patrol Unit operation at a Unitedville residence.

Police have not disclosed the full circumstances surrounding Thursday’s incident or whether anyone sustained injuries.

World.title: Belize prepares commitments to end violence against children
World.content:
Belize prepares commitments to end violence against children

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Belize is getting ready to present new commitments on ending violence against children on the world stage.

On Thursday, October 8, the Government held a National Preparatory Session at the Belize Biltmore Plaza in Belize City. The dialogue was organized by the Ministry of Human Development, Family Support and Gender Affairs, the Ministry of Health and Wellness and the Office of the Special Envoy for the Development of Families and Children, with support from UNICEF and PAHO/WHO.

Government officials, civil society, development partners, technical experts, children and young people took part.

The session will help shape Belize’s position ahead of the Second Global Ministerial Conference on Ending Violence Against Children, set for November 18 and 19 in Manila, Philippines.

Participants reviewed progress since the first conference in Bogotá, Colombia, in 2024, where Belize pledged to speed up efforts to end violence against children.

The dialogue focused on taking stock of progress, hearing from children and civil society, identifying achievable actions and building consensus on a national package of commitments.

Minister Garcia-Ramirez said the true measure of success will be what changes for children in Belize after the conference.

“Every child in Belize has the right to grow up safe, protected, and heard,” she said.

World.title: Third murder reported in Belize City in less than 48 hours as gun violence grips Southside
World.content:
Third murder reported in Belize City in less than 48 hours as gun violence grips Southside

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Belize City has reportedly recorded its third murder in less than 48 hours following a shooting on Central American Boulevard on Friday night.

Preliminary reports indicate that police responded to gunfire in the area and that a shooting victim was rushed to the Karl Heusner Memorial Hospital (KHMH). The victim has been identified as Jory Bowen, who is reportedly deceased. However, official confirmation of his death and the circumstances surrounding the shooting remains pending.

The latest shooting follows two murders on Thursday, October 8. Seventeen-year-old Kaylon David was shot on Iguana Street Extension around 6:30 p.m. and later died at the hospital. Approximately three hours later, 20-year-old Shamar Smith was gunned down on Pelican Street by an assailant who reportedly arrived on a motorcycle. Both incidents remain under investigation.

Following those killings, Assistant Commissioner of Police Hilberto Romero acknowledged concerns about possible retaliatory violence and said police were launching operations and holding meetings to prevent further bloodshed. Investigators have not established any connection between Friday night’s shooting and the two earlier murders.

Police have yet to release further details on the latest incident.

World.title: Belize Coast Guard officer earns Naval Nursing degree
World.content:
Belize Coast Guard officer earns Naval Nursing degree

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): The Belize Coast Guard has a new nursing graduate in its ranks.

Lieutenant Junior Grade Elvis Soliz has completed his Bachelor’s Degree in Naval Nursing at the Centro de Estudios Navales en Ciencias de la Salud in Mexico City, graduating on Saturday.

The August Pine Ridge native has steadily built his academic record. He earned his associate’s degree in Biology and Natural Resource Management from Centro Escolar Mexico Junior College in 2022, where he made the Honor Roll.

Now, he brings new healthcare skills to his service with the Coast Guard.

His journey shows what dedication to education and service can achieve, and it is an inspiration to young people in August Pine Ridge and across Belize.

Congratulations to Lt JG Soliz. May his career in service and healthcare bring even greater success.

World.title: Reggae Girlz defeat Mexico 4-3 in friendly
World.content:
Jamaica's midfielder #14 Deneisha Blackwood celebrates scoring her team's third goal during the women's international friendly football match between Mexico and Jamaica at Victoria stadium in Aguascalientes, Mexico, on October 9, 2026. (Photo: AFP)

Jamaica’s Reggae Girlz outscored Mexico 4-3 in the first of two friendly internationals in Aguascalientes on Friday as they stepped up preparations for their Concacaf Women’s Championship quarter-final against Costa Rica.

Jamaica led 2-0 after 20 minutes but the hosts kept clawing their way back with timely goals that kept the contest close.

It was the first time the Reggae Girlz scored four goals in a game against a North American opposition and the first time since 2022 that Jamaica beat Mexico in senior women’s football.

Jodi Brown gave Jamaica the lead in the 15th minute when she finished off a good move started by Khadija ‘Bunny’ Shaw. Shaw dribbled from her own half deep into the Mexican half before passing the ball to Paige Bailey-Gayle on the left of the 18-yard box. Bailey-Gayle then played the ball into the path of Brown who fired into the goal.

Shaw then fired home from the left side of the 18-yard box, her 67th goal in national colours, to make it 2-0.

Mexico pulled a goal back in the 29th minute when Lizbeth Ovalle got her boot to a cross from the right side, guiding it past goalkeeper Rebecca Spencer.

Jamaica restored their two goals lead when referee Sandra Benitez Arteaga awarded a penalty after Shaw was fouled in the box, and Deneisha Blackwood made no mistake from the spot in the 36th minute.

Once again Mexico would cut the deficit when Manchester United midfielder Rebeca Bernal, the Mexican captain, headed a cross from the right side into the goal at the far post.

Mexico could have drawn level late but hit the base of the left post.

Solai Washington, who replaced Bailey-Gayle at the start of the second half, had a good chance to score but she fired straight at goalkeeper Esthefanny Barreras in the 55th minute.

Mexico had two other good chances to pull level but Spencer made two good saves, the best in the 85th minute when she went to her left to parry a shot from point blank range.

However, Washington made up for her earlier miss in the 90th minute, finishing off a move that saw Jamaica holding the ball for more than two minutes.

The host would not go away and found another goal, arguably the best of the seven that were scored, when Charlyn Coralle curled a shot from about 22 yards out and into the far right corner in the fifth minute of time added.

-Paul A Reid

World.title: We deserve more!
World.content:
Visitors and Jamaicans enjoying Doctor’s Cave Beach in Montego Bay St James.

MONTEGO BAY, St James — Arguing that the city of Montego Bay punches well above its weight in bringing in tourism dollars, St James Municipal Corporation Chairman Richard Vernon wants the parish to be given a larger share of revenue generated by the Tourism Enhancement Fund (TEF).

“We deserve — based on the impact that tourism is creating on the local economy and the physical infrastructure of Montego Bay — to get a share of tourism dollars,” Vernon said, referencing revenue largely generated from a portion of air and cruise fees added to central government’s consolidated fund.

The mayor made the argument Thursday evening as he headlined the corporation’s town hall budget presentation held at Montego Bay Cultural Centre, in the heart of the tourist resort city.

Vernon, who is also mayor, laid out the sources of income and the expenditure that will make up the city’s $2.8-billion budget for the 2027-2028 financial year.

The bulk of spending will go to administration, which will receive $709 million.

According to Vernon, this is how much it costs to run the municipal corporation.

“It pays for the people who approve building plans, issue permits, pay the bills, keep the records, and answer when residents call,” a slide from his presentation states.

Other planned expenditure include street lighting, which was listed at $337 million, garbage collection at $476 million, and road repairs at $172 million.

Vernon put planned capital expenditure for the period at $1.086 billion, with one of the key projects being the long-awaited upgrade of a vendors’ arcade in the city centre.

“To improve conditions for vendors, support business activity, and create an attractive, orderly retail space, we are allocating $200 million for the physical rehabilitation of the Old Shoe Market to get much of our vendors off the streets,” he explained.

The municipal corporation will also undertake work at Charles Gordon Market, with $160 million earmarked for infrastructure upgrades to that facility.

Another $100 million will be allocated for structural repairs and upgrades to the Montego Bay Transportation Centre, with the aim of improving connectivity for thousands of workers and students who use the facility daily.

Vernon also highlighted plans to improve sidewalks, signage, murals, and other infrastructure through the corporation’s Urban Development Programme, which has been allocated $400 million.

He stressed that St James needs additional funding, which he believes could be secured through greater support from the TEF.

“While we have good partners, and while we have a good, robust professional relationship with the Tourism Enhancement Fund and Ministry of Tourism, we believe that Montego Bay is entitled,” argued Vernon.

The TEF has generated billions of dollars since it was set up more than 20 years ago, fuelled by fees of US$20 and US$2, respectively, from each incoming airline and cruise passenger.

In the 2023/24 fiscal year, the fund is reported to have collected approximately US$59.2 million.

On Thursday, while justifying his advocacy for an increased slice of the TEF pie for Montego Bay, Vernon said, “We have 30 per cent of all the rooms in the country, we have the largest airport in the English-speaking Caribbean, and we are responsible for 70 per cent of all flights into Jamaica.

Whether they arrive via cruise ships or by air, Montego Bay manages 70 per cent of that.” He argued that additional funding was needed to maintain the city’s infrastructure as visitor numbers continued to grow.

“We have a transient population of approximately two million people annually even though Statin (Statistical Institute of Jamaica) is saying that we are close to 200,000 people.

We have two million because 1.5 million tourists reside in Montego Bay annually in our hotels,” the mayor explained.

“They use the water, they use the sewerage systems, they use the roads, it impacts the local economy.

Therefore, to maintain the pace at which Montego Bay is growing and going re: tourism, we need a share of dollars to ensure we fix up our city properly,” he insisted.

The call for more of tourism- generated revenue to be spent in resort areas is not new.

For years members of the business community and locally elected representatives in Hanover and Westmoreland have made a similar request regarding expenditure for Negril.

For now, faced with the reality of the funds available, the mayor told the town hall meeting how the corporation intends to finance its budget of more than $2 billion.

“Our baseline projections are driven by public taxes, which stands as our largest share at $1.29 billion,” Vernon stated.

“This is supported by central government subvention from the consolidated fund at $650 million, local user fees at $561 million, and motor vehicle licences at $350 million.

When combined, these projected streams fulfil all operational mandates,” he said.

Vernon stressed that there were no new taxes being imposed at the local level for the next fiscal year, while efforts are being made to identify other revenue-generating measures and boost efficiency.

The TEF was established in 2005 to implement recommendations emanating from the Master Plan for Sustainable Tourism Development.

In 2018, it was restructured to operate as a centre for innovation for tourism, with responsibility for strategic and targeted projects that support key activities aimed at realising growth targets.

At the launch of the Montego Bay Chamber of Commerce Expo in 2019, TEF Chairman Godfrey Dyer outlined the numerous projects to which the fund has contributed in Montego Bay.

“I can say with pride that the Tourism Enhancement Fund has done more for Montego Bay than you know,” Dyer said.

He pointed to the construction of a state-of-the-art beach park at Closed Harbour Beach in Montego Bay is one of a number of pioneering initiatives that the agency has endorsed in the city.

Additionally, it contributed $700 million towards the funding of the major development on the 16-acre property commonly known as Dump-up Beach.

The TEF also provided support the National Works Agency and the St James Municipal Corporation’s road improvement programmes over the years, among them the construction of sidewalks and verges on Harbour Street and Jimmy Cliff Boulevard, as well as the paving of Kent Avenue, which leads to the popular Dead End Beach.

The TEF has also funded the municipality’s sidewalk rehabilitation programme and drainage systems along a number of streets throughout downtown Montego Bay.

Dyer also pointed out that the TEF has given the city that Montego Bay Cultural Centre in historic Sam Sharpe Square.

“You must also know that the Tourism Enhancement Fund is responsible for rescuing a historic landmark and the source of Montego Bay’s first case of domestic water supply, the Creek Dome.

The repairs of the dome were done by us,” Dyer said.

Additionally, the TEF has provided support to education, providing hands-on learning for students to develop real-life skills.

Montego Bay Community College, Mount Alvernia High, and Montego Bay High are among the schools that have benefited from TEF’s financial commitments.

Dyer also told his audience that the TEF “has enabled repairs to the St James Municipal Corporation and the St James Parish Church as well as the Burchell Baptist Church…

So we are touching the lives in every area,” Dyer said.

The TEF has reported that for the 2026/27 fiscal year it has dedicated allocations including $1.4 billion for public beach and road attraction maintenance, alongside specific capital allocations such as $456 million toward the St James Municipal Corporation’s urban renewal and capital programmes.

World.title: Grieving deputy fire chief urges Jamaicans to unite against road carnage
World.content:
A motor vehicle involved in a fatal crash in St James. (Photo: Observer file)

MONTEGO BAY, St James — New St James deputy fire chief Superintendent O’Neil Henry is all too familiar with the carnage that can take place on the roads, having recently lost his son and his son’s girlfriend in a crash.

With that memory still fresh in his mind, Henry used Thursday’s monthly meeting of the St James Municipal Corporation to call for a united approach to addressing the problem.

Henry attributed the crashes to a combination of poor road conditions and dangerous driving.

“We have to find a way, in conjunction with the police, to educate these drivers who are driving on the road,” he urged.

“We know that speeding will kill and it will hurt, so the Jamaica Fire Brigade, in collaboration with the Jamaica Constabulary Force (JCF), the other ministries, other agencies, and the St James Municipal Corporation, we have to find a way to reach out to those persons within our scope and see how we can educate them on driving safely,” added Henry.

According to Henry, his team was among first responders at seven crashes in September, down from 12 in August.

However, added to his concerns is an out-of-service ambulance that has left his team hobbled.

“Our emergency medical service (EMS) is currently not in operation due to our ambulance having an accident.

We are repairing the ambulance, we are working on it.

In short order we will have that ambulance up and running, and that also will help in our service when it comes on to, especially, motor vehicle accidents,” the senior firefighter said.

In responding to his passionate appeal, Deputy Mayor Dwight Crawford told the meeting of Henry’s recent loss.

His son O’Neil Henry Jr and his girlfriend, 25- year-old Alicia Dormer of Westgate Hills in St James, died from injuries sustained in a crash on the Braco main road in Trelawny on August 17.

“We issue our condolence to you and the family,” said Crawford as other councillors added their expressions of sympathy.

In accepting their show of support Henry reiterated his appeal for a joint approach to addressing the problem.

“We are asking for us to be a unit and try to see how much we can assist in lessening motor vehicle accidents in our parish and in our surroundings,” he said.

In its latest update the Island Traffic Authority (ITA) reported that as of October 9 Jamaica has recorded 227 fatal crashes, resulting in the loss of 263 lives.

This represents a 13 per cent reduction when compared to the corresponding period in 2025.

Manager of corporate communications and public relations at the ITA Dontae Matthews urged all road users to remain alert in their daily commute, and shared that the entity is fully committed to supporting targeted enforcement initiatives and continuing public education efforts to promote safer road usage.

“Through sustained collaboration with public and private sector partners, the authority will continue to champion initiatives that encourage lasting behaviour change and help reduce preventable crashes and fatalities,” said Matthews.

World.title: AfroSzn heats up Dubwise Café
World.content:
AfroSzn promoters DJ Denvo (left), Sashana Lamont, and DJ Powa pause for a photo op.

At the recent staging of AfroSzn, which took place at Dubwise Café, it was evident that the event continues to carve out a unique space in Kingston’s nightlife scene.

AfroSzn’s fourth staging transformed Dubwise Café into a vibrant celebration of African rhythms and culture, featuring a captivating performance by the Djembe-Kon Cultural Performing Arts Group and a guest appearance from the Dancehall Family Tree (DFT).

What began as a passion project between DJs searching for something different has evolved into a growing community united by a shared appreciation for African music genres such as Amapiano, GQOM, 3Step, Lekompo, Afro House, and Afro Tech.

“The inspiration behind AfroSzn was the music.

It all started with the music,” DJ Denvo, one of the organisers told the Jamaica Observer.

“As DJs, we reached a point where we wanted to play something different, not just the regular music you hear every day on the radio or at events.

We were experiencing what you could call DJ burnout, and during that time we discovered Amapiano, 3Step, GQOM, and other sounds coming out of South Africa.

It felt different. It felt spiritual.

It was music we connected with.” According to DJ Powa, another member of the organising team, introducing new elements at each event has become an important part of the AfroSzn formula.

“For every staging we try to create a special item that excites our audience,” he said.

“In the past, we’ve incorporated live drum pads, had drummers performing throughout the night, and even created an Afro House remix of the popular WYFL rhythms.

This time we featured live drummers and dancers from the Djembe-Kon Cultural Performing Arts Group.” DJ Denvo said AfroSzn has evolved since its initial staging.

“Since the first staging, AfroSzn has grown beyond just being a space where we play Afro music, and we’ve seen more people become familiar with the different genres and sounds that we play.

The events have also evolved in how we present the music and the overall experience.

We are becoming more intentional about incorporating different elements of African and Jamaican culture, while still keeping the music at the centre.

Each staging gives us an opportunity to introduce something new while maintaining what people have come to know AfroSzn for,” he reasoned.

Asked what patrons can expect when they attend AfroSzn, he said: “Patrons can expect excellent music, pure Afro energy, and an experience that takes them on a journey through different sounds from the African continent.

The music is carefully curated from beginning to end, so it’s not just about playing a collection of songs.

We want people to discover new music, connect with the sounds, and, most importantly, have a good time.

The people who come are genuinely there for the music and the experience, creating a strong sense of community.” The next staging of AfroSzn is scheduled for November 26 at Dubwise Café.

World.title: Red Stripe and NRSC ink partnership to advance road safety
World.content:
National Road Safety Council Executive Director Paula Fletcher (seated, left) and Red Stripe Managing Director Holly Bostock sign a memorandum of understanding to advance road safety initiatives in Jamaica, at Red Stripe’s Spanish Town Road office on Tuesday. Looking on are Dianne Ashton Smith (standing, left), head of corporate affairs, Red Stripe; and Daika Mitchell, communications manager, internal and sustainability, Red Stripe.

RED Stripe and the National Road Safety Council (NRSC) have formalised a partnership to strengthen road safety efforts across Jamaica, in support of the United Nations Decade of Action for Road Safety 2021-2030.

The organisations signed a memorandum of understanding (MOU) on Tuesday at Red Stripe’s Spanish Town Road offices, establishing a framework for continued collaboration on road safety initiatives aimed at encouraging responsible decision-making and safer communities.

Nearly 1.2 million people lose their lives in road crashes globally each year, while between 20 and 50 million suffer serious, often life-changing injuries.

The Global Plan for the Decade of Action for Road Safety calls for a holistic approach that prioritises safety across all aspects of road system design, planning and management, with a goal of reducing road traffic deaths and injuries by 50 per cent by 2030.

In Jamaica, the partnership brings together Red Stripe’s Drink & Live Responsibly platform and the NRSC’s national road safety mandate to promote responsible choices around alcohol consumption, transportation and social occasions.

Speaking at the signing ceremony, NRSC Executive Director Paula Fletcher underscored the importance of partnerships in tackling Jamaica’s road safety challenges.

“Road safety cannot be addressed by one organisation or sector alone.

We need partnerships that take the message into the spaces where people live, work and socialise, and that encourage individuals to think about how their choices affect themselves and others.

“Behaviour change takes consistent engagement, and partnerships with the private sector can help us reach people in meaningful and practical ways,” said Fletcher.

Red Stripe Managing Director Holly Bostock said the partnership builds on the company’s long-standing commitment to promoting responsibility.

“Living responsibly has always been a core value at Red Stripe, and we wanted to take that commitment further by putting greater focus on the choices that can protect people and communities.

Guh Easy gives us a platform to do that, and our partnership with the NRSC allows us to take a firm stand on road safety and encourage practical action,” said Bostock.

The first initiative under the partnership is Guh Easy Heroes, a public recognition programme that will celebrate Jamaicans who demonstrate responsibility and make positive contributions to the safety and well-being of others.

Announcing the initiative, Dianne Ashton-Smith, head of corporate Affairs at Red Stripe, said the programme aims to highlight the everyday actions that often go unnoticed but can have a lasting impact.

“Road safety is often discussed in terms of statistics and consequences, but at its heart it is about people and the decisions they make.

Every day, Jamaicans make choices that help keep others safe, but those actions rarely get recognised.

Through Guh Easy Heroes we want to celebrate the people who quietly look out for others and show what responsibility looks like in practice,” said Ashton-Smith.

Jamaicans can nominate a Guh Easy Hero by commenting on the campaign post on Red Stripe corporate’s social media pages, tagging the nominee, identifying their parish, and sharing why they deserve recognition.

Nominations opened on October 7 and close on October 13.

Nominees may include designated drivers, people who arrange transportation for others, or individuals who consistently encourage family members, friends and colleagues to make safer decisions.

A joint panel comprising representatives of Red Stripe and the NRSC will select one hero from each parish, taking into account the nominee’s actions, their impact on others, and their ability to encourage responsible behaviour within their communities.

The 14 heroes will be announced on National Heroes’ Day.

Their stories will then be featured on Red Stripe’s social media platforms, where members of the public will have the opportunity to vote for the 2026 Guh Easy People’s Choice Hero.

The winner will be recognised at a special luncheon later in October.

Each hero will receive a commemorative plaque, official recognition as a 2026 Guh Easy Hero, VIP access for two to a premium Red Stripe experience, round-trip transportation to and from the recognition event, and a Guh Easy Hero Experience Package containing branded merchandise, keepsakes and curated gifts.

Heroes will also be recognised through Red Stripe and NRSC communication channels.

The MOU provides a framework for Red Stripe and the NRSC to continue working together on future initiatives that encourage responsible choices and contribute to Jamaica’s broader road safety goals.

World.title: Mayor declares war on litterbugs
World.content:
A section of the garbage-strewn drain that runs alongside the Falmouth Transformation Centre in Trelawny

FALMOUTH, Trelawny — Tired of being blamed for filthy conditions in the parish capital — despite the municipal authority’s ongoing efforts to keep the town clean — chairman of the Trelawny Municipal Corporation (TMC) C Junior Gager says a major clean-up is being planned, alongside tougher measures to punish litterbugs.

Gager said the corporation will be working with the National Solid Waste Management Authority (NSWMA), the health department, and the police to tackle indiscriminate dumping, particularly in Water Square and the town’s bus park.

Speaking during Thursday’s regular monthly meeting of the TMC, Gager warned that vendors who fail to maintain proper sanitation standards could be removed from Water Square, while people caught littering could face prosecution.

“It is the responsibility of those who use Water Square to keep it clean.

Those who are selling, if you don’t have a bag to put your garbage in, you should not be selling there.

You should also be required to keep your surroundings clean,” Gager said.

He appealed to vendors to take greater responsibility for the conduct of their customers by encouraging them to use the garbage receptacles provided, rather than leaving bottles and other waste scattered around the square.

Gager also urged members of the public to get involved in naming and shaming litterbugs.

“Once you see someone that decides that they’d want to discard garbage any and everywhere, just take a picture and send it to us.

We are going to be having a page, and we are going to be naming you.

I hope it will shame you, and to say keep the place clean,” he said.

The mayor expressed particular concern about plastic drink bottles being carelessly discarded, creating additional work for municipal crews.

“If you look and you go by the bus park, one of the greatest disasters is that when you drink, you just throw down the bottles.

In no time at all the wind comes; they are blown into the drain, and all of these bottles keep swimming, swimming in the drain,” added Gager.

He argued that while social media users play an important role in highlighting problems in the town, some fail to appreciate the resources being spent to maintain public spaces and clear drains.

“We could do something else with it [money] if everyone was just cooperative and, as you pass, you drop your bottle into the bin that is provided,” Gager said.

Following reports that some people pay handymen or cart men to remove garbage, only for it to be dumped in unauthorised locations, Gager said the municipal corporation intends to work with NSWMA to monitor how businesses dispose of their waste.

“We are going to start tracing some of these garbage and see where it is coming from,” he vowed.

The mayor also raised concern about food waste being discarded by vendors, particularly those selling soup and chicken, warning that the practice attracts rats and contributes to the growing rodent problem in the town.

“You throw it by the roadside, you throw it in a culvert, the rats come out and eat it, so they multiply fast — and they are all over the town.

We cannot allow this, so we’ll have to put some strong measures in place,” warned Gager.

He said the planned clean-up would not just be a one-time event and there are plans to ensure that improvements are sustained, with residents, vendors, and business operators playing their part in keeping Falmouth clean.

World.title: UHWI puts lived experience at centre of Mental Health Week
World.content:
Members of the University Hospital of the West Indies (UHWI) Department of Psychiatry pose for a photograph during the launch of Mental Health Week 2026. The week of activities, held under the theme ‘Lived Experiences Heard: Real Voices, Real Change’, seeks to amplify the voices of people with lived experiences of mental health challenges while promoting greater awareness, understanding and inclusion.

THE University Hospital of the West Indies (UHWI) is putting the voices and experiences of people affected by mental health challenges at the centre of its Mental Health Week, launched on Monday by the hospital’s Department of Psychiatry.

The launch brought together members of the UHWI leadership team and representatives of departments across the hospital as the institution began a weeklong programme of discussions, wellness activities and public engagement.

Mental Health Week is being held in observance of World Mental Health Day, recognised annually on October 10, and is guided this year by the global theme, ‘Lived Experiences Heard: Real Voices, Real Change’.

Dr Clayton Sewell, head of the Department of Psychiatry at UHWI, said the theme challenges health-care providers and the wider society to think more carefully about whose voices are included in conversations about mental health.

“Too often, we talk about people experiencing mental health challenges instead of talking with them.

Their experiences provide insight that clinical training alone cannot, and those voices have an important place in how we think about care, recovery, and the support people need.

Mental Health Week gives us an opportunity to listen, challenge some of the stigma that still surrounds mental illness, and keep mental health as part of the wider conversation about health and well-being,” Sewell said.

The programme will culminate today, World Mental Health Day, with a family forum and health fair from 10:00 am to 3:00 pm — providing another opportunity for families and the wider community to engage in conversations around mental health and well-being.

At UHWI, the Department of Psychiatry provides inpatient and outpatient mental health services across a range of specialities while also supporting the training of medical and other health-care professionals through The University of the West Indies.

The week was also intended to keep conversations about mental health going beyond the clinical setting, with patients, families and the wider community part of that discussion.

World.title: POWER PLAY
World.content:
West Indies players celebrate the dismissal of Tom Latham (not pictured) of New Zealand during the fourth One-Day International cricket match at Kensington Oval in Bridgetown, Barbados, on July 19, 2026. (Photo: AFP)

WITH Cricket West Indies (CWI) undergoing major financial restructuring, former Australia captain and two-time World Cup winner Michael Clarke believes the International Cricket Council (ICC), along with India, Australia and England, must urgently step in to help rescue cricket in the Caribbean.

Two weeks ago CWI announced a series of changes to tackle their current financial crisis, which was highlighted by the 25 per cent reduction in retainer fees for the West Indies’ men’s and women’s team.

Domestic players, including 15 Jamaicans, will also see their contracts cut from 12 months to seven months amid the suspension of the Super 50 tournament and the reduction of the four-day tournament.

CWI Chief Executive Officer (CEO), Jamaican Chris Dehring, in addressing the changes, said “it is a necessary step towards financial stability”.

However Clarke, who won the 2007 and 2015 World Cup, believes the top stakeholders of the sport shouldn’t stand by to watch the Windies struggle.

“I’m really concerned for West Indies cricket,” he told the Beyond 23 Cricket Podcast.

“Honestly, this is where I think, firstly, the ICC, but even if it’s the big three — India, Australia, and England — need to come together to save West Indies cricket,” he said.

The 45-year-old Clarke, who scored over 16000 runs across Test and One-Day Internationals (ODIs) in his 11-year career, says he’s always been concerned about the West Indies’ situation for over a decade.

“If West Indies are not the lowest-paid nation, they’re in the conversation.

I go back to the conversation I had when the IPL started in its first or second year, when Chris Gayle got crit- icism for choosing IPL over West Indies,” he said.

“He was the highest-paid West Indies player on 100,000 US dollars a year, 12-month contract.

He signed a deal at the IPL for a million dollars US at that week, at that stage, for a four-and-a-half or six-week tournament.

How could he say no to that deal? You couldn’t have a go at Chris for making that decision, and he played his backside off for West Indies as well.” Clarke, who scored a century and three half-centuries in 12 Tests against the West Indies, says an immediate intervention is needed to save the current crop of players.

“These West Indies players, they’re already getting paid the lowest amount or close to it.

[If] you take 25 per cent of their money away how do they not just turn into a franchise player, play five or six different franchises around the world, and say, ‘Unfortunately, we’ll play for the West Indies but we’re not going to sign a central contract’? “You can’t blame them.

I just think they need help, and the ICC and the three big nations have just got to find a way, in my opinion.” Former England spinner Monty Panesar, who took 167 in 50 Tests, says the current squad should try their best to prove their worth on the pitch.

“Distractions aren’t going to help the West Indies players.

And that’s going to be the key thing — how they put that aside and not worry about the payment issues, the financial crisis that West Indies cricket is at the moment,” he said.

[They should say,] ‘Let’s grab these opportunities, let’s find a couple of youngsters, a couple of gems from this tour in India, and let’s take on India.

Let’s not be afraid of the sort of superstars of Indian cricket, and let’s take on the ecosystem of the media as well.’ “We know Indian media, there’s a hyper focus on how great this Indian team is, how good they are in India, and [yet] look at what Australia did.

They beat India in India during the World Cup.

That’s the inspiration that West Indies cricket should take to say, as players, let’s make an impact on this tour.” The Windies are currently locked at 1-1 in the five match T20 series against India, following Friday’s impressive six-wicket win.

Daren Sammy’s men are coming off a 2-1 ODI series loss to the Indians last week.

World.title: Germany warns EU that €159B budget cuts are not enough
World.content:
“We are still a long way from an agreement. The amount of the new proposal is not a basis for an agreement. The EU budget must be affordable for those who bear the brunt of the financing,” Merz wrote in a statement on Saturday.

Germany leads a group of six “frugal” countries — Sweden, Denmark, the Netherlands, Finland and Austria — which contribute 40% of the Union’s common budget.

Most frugal countries criticized Ireland’s proposed €159 billion in cuts in current prices from the Commission’s nearly €2 trillion proposal, saying they were insufficient.

Sweden’s Europe minister Jessica Rosencrantz described the negotiating document, or negobox, on X as a “wildly unaffordable increase,” as the overall amount would still be higher than the current budget.

Austrian Europe Minister Claudia Bauer echoed that criticism, saying that the new budget remained "miles away from an Austrian yes.”

Tensions will come to a head during a summit of EU leaders next Thursday and Friday, where they will discuss the negobox.

World.title: Strikes killing 17 are Russia’s ‘thanks’ for US diesel sanctions lift, Zelenskyy says
World.content:
“Today, Russia expressed its thanks for the lifting of sanctions on diesel exports by dropping five glide bombs on residential buildings in Zaporizhzhia,” Zelenskyy said on X.

The strikes took place just one day after U.S. President Donald Trump announced he would temporarily lift sanctions on Russian diesel in a bid to bring soaring prices down.

Ukrainian officials were meeting on the same day with European and U.S. officials in Miami in a fresh diplomatic push to end the conflict between Russia and Ukraine.

Zelenskyy criticized the deal on Friday and accused Trump of using the peace talks as a “smokescreen” while pursuing a deal with the Kremlin.

Even though the talks were supposed to last two days, the Ukrainian team decided to return home earlier then planned “because they managed to talk everything through earlier,” a senior official familiar with the matter told POLITICO. Ukraine will continue to bomb Russian oil refineries despite US-Russia deals, the official added.

The Ukrainian armed forces said Saturday they struck a major oil facility in Russia’s Samara region overnight.

World.title: Turkey bans social media for kids under 15
World.content:
The law also includes provisions for minors over 15, stating that platforms cannot offer them services that could have "an addictive effect."

Turkey has often implemented tough restrictions on social media services, frequently banning individual accounts from media outlets or activists, and at times banning access to entire platforms. Ankara banned Instagram for a week in 2024 amid claims the Meta-owned platform censored users mourning Hamas leader Ismail Haniyeh.

Last week Turkey blocked a news website and its social media accounts over what a court deemed to be "LGBT propaganda," sparking outrage from human rights and media freedom groups.

A 2025 report from the U.S.-based think tank Freedom House described Turkey's internet as "not free."

Turkey joins a growing group of states, including Australia and Indonesia, that are introducing or exploring tougher age restrictions on social media access.

In September the European Union presented a legal proposal to restrict children's access to social media and video-sharing platforms until they turn 15, following months of intense pressure from EU leaders on the issue.

Austria, Denmark, France, Greece and Spain are all pushing ahead with national laws to restrict kids' access to social media. The United Kingdom is also expected to introduce a ban next year.

Canada has also presented a bill to restrict access to social media platforms for children under 16.

World.title: EU budget slashed by €159B in new Irish proposal
World.content:
The bloc is split between frugal countries demanding cuts of several hundred billions to the nearly €2 trillion proposal on the table and a rival camp of southern and eastern states, known as the Friends of Cohesion, opposing reductions.

In a concession to the Friends of Cohesion, Ireland shielded farmers’ subsidies and regional payouts, that account for half of the total budget and are politically sensitive, from any cuts.

Instead, the bulk of the reductions came from foreign aid which was cut by €38 billion; competitiveness which was axed by €75 billion and the EU’s administrative costs which were reduced by €10 billion.

Dublin also scrapped a rainy day fund, known as the "EU Facility cushion," that allowed the European Commission to deploy cash to tackle unforeseen emergencies throughout the seven-year budget cycle.

Ireland’s Minister of State for European Affairs Thomas Byrne, who leads the negotiations, defended the proposal as a balanced compromise between 27 countries.

“We protected … the traditional policies of the Union, which are very important for the European Union and the single market. But we also very much look to the future,” Byrne told reporters.

Wie lässt sich der industrielle Kern des Landes retten, bevor die internationale Wettbewerbsfähigkeit endgültig wegbricht? Der niedersächsische SPD-Ministerpräsident Olaf Lies liefert in der Talk-Reihe „Let’s find common ground“ von POLITICO die Bestandsaufnahme einer Industrie am Scheideweg.

Er erklärt, warum das europäische Lieferkettengesetz jetzt zwingend ausgesetzt werden muss und weshalb der ständige Streit um kurzfristige Erfolge das Vertrauen in die demokratische Mitte zermürbt.

World.title: UK bans Protestant march from Catholic area in Northern Ireland
World.content:
“I call for all protests, rallies and demonstrations to be stood down. There is no excuse for a continued ratcheting up of tensions,” Bryant appealed in a statement explaining why he was reversing the original decision by the Parades Commission, Northern Ireland’s independent body for managing the region’s chronic conflicts over Orange Order demonstrations.

Street fighting over those traditional marches helped to trigger the onset of Northern Ireland’s three-decade conflict, known as “The Troubles,” which left nearly 3,700 dead before a 1998 peace accord.

Hundreds of Catholic locals backed by Sinn Féin, the Irish republican party that leads Northern Ireland’s fraying cross-community government, gathered along the Garvaghy Road in Portadown to cheer the reversal.

First Minister Michelle O’Neill, who has been accused of breaking the law while helping locals block the Orangemen’s intended path since Sept. 27, went on Ireland’s flagship TV talk show, the Late Late Show, to express relief on behalf of the residents of Garvaghy Road.

“For the last 13 days they’ve been living with this constant fear and a cloud hanging over them that this unwanted sectarian march was going to be forced down that road,” she said.

But the main pro-British party in the coalition, the Democratic Unionists, denounced Bryant’s move as a capitulation to mob rule. Some DUP lawmakers called for Northern Ireland’s police chief, who had recommended the policy reversal, to be fired.

Democratic Unionist leader Gavin Robinson said the U.K. government had sent a dangerous message that Northern Ireland “should be run on force of numbers and who shouts the loudest.”

Northern Ireland’s nearly three-decade system for managing conflict over parades “now lies in tatters,” he said, “and the rule of law has been fundamentally undermined.”

World.title: Ryanair lashes out at Air France and Lufthansa over ownership probe
World.content:
The association confirmed to POLITICO that it has spent months urging EU and Irish aviation authorities to investigate whether Ryanair complies with the bloc’s ownership and control rules.

Under those rules, airlines must be majority-owned and effectively controlled by EU nationals or entities to hold an EU operating license. ENAA argues that Ryanair no longer meets those requirements, pointing to the airline’s March announcement that only 30% of its shares are held by EU nationals. O'Leary, an Irish citizen, holds 4% of the stock.

When the Irish Aviation Authority seemed “reluctant to engage on the matter,” ENAA took the matter to court. If Ryanair loses the case, it could be forced to change its ownership structure. The carrier's operating license would only be suspended if it does not comply with the verdict.

An aircraft operated by Irish low cost airline Ryanair makes its way past BER airport's control tower in Schoenefeld on June 29, 2026. | John Macdougall/AFP via Getty Images

Ryanair has rejected the allegations, arguing that its non-EU shareholders do not have voting rights, which means the airline is under EU control.

In an emailed statement, Ryanair accused its rivals of attempting “to restrict competition and choice for EU air travel” by challenging its operating license.

Grounding risk seen as remote

Augusto Viansson Ponte, a London-based director at Alton Aviation Consultancy, doubted that the legal case would be easily dismissed, but also said it was unlikely that Ryanair would lose its operating license.

World.title: Arrested German spy chief lashed out at his old agency over allegations he spied for Russia
World.content:
Jäger did not respond to the letter at the time, according to Hanning, who spoke to WELT before his arrest.

Hanning’s subsequent arrest, including on suspicion of attempted treason, has caused considerable concern abroad. Grzegorz Malecki, the former head of Poland’s foreign intelligence service, told WELT that the case was “extremely concerning” and could deepen allies’ distrust of the BND. He warned this had the potential to undermine intelligence-sharing with Germany.

The BND has also raised eyebrows within Germany’s intelligence community over allegations that it allowed Hanning’s former chief of staff, who is also in custody, to work for Hanning outside his official duties.

While civil servants are generally permitted to take on outside employment, any approval allowing a member of the BND to work for Hanning would have had to be decided at the senior management level, said Günter Heiss, a former intelligence coordinator under former Chancellor Angela Merkel. “Without knowing the details, I would never have approved anything like this had I been in a position of responsibility at the BND.”

Bernd Schmidbauer, a former minister of state and intelligence coordinator under Chancellor Helmut Kohl, told WELT that Hanning had made major contributions to Germany’s national security. The affair was therefore “not only a tragedy for the German intelligence services, but also for the former senior official himself,” Schmidbauer said.

Hanning was among Schmidbauer’s closest aides during the 1990s and went on to lead the BND from 1998 to 2005.

Dirk Banse is an investigative reporter at WELT. Philipp Fritz is WELT’s Eastern Europe correspondent. Uwe Müller is a freelance reporter based in Berlin.
