World.title: Songlines, ceremony and small steps: The search for hope among the men of Alice Springs
World.content:
Amid intense scrutiny over family violence, local leaders and elders are getting young Indigenous men back on Country to reclaim culture and responsibilities.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

After days of dreary rain following Kumanjayi Little Baby’s funeral, the veil of grief and Sorry Business eases over Alice Springs. The men at Red Dust Role Models, a non-profit mentoring organisation for Indigenous people, have organised an impromptu gathering in the foothills of the East MacDonnell ranges – Country of the Black Caterpillar dreaming, Tyape Utnerrengatye. Red Dust, along with community leaders and local men, have sought to give this masthead an understanding of the plight of men in Alice Springs, and the wider central desert region. To explore the complexity of issues that lead to, but do not excuse, the extreme rates of domestic, family and sexual violence in the community. Now they are on Country, amid a stunning and monumental landscape. The Black Caterpillar Dreaming story of the ranges stretches out along the landscape to beyond the horizon, adorned in vibrant hues of red, pink and yellow desert blooms and vivid green tussock grass after the rain. Traditional owner Damien Kunoth arrives early with his son Byson. The men walk the land in the way of their ancestors, along songlines, acknowledging sacred sites and searching for food; for bush banana (upali) and bush coconut (kandar), which are in abundance, but past their best. Traditional owner Damien Kunoth (Arrernte) with son Byson on country outside Alice Springs. Justin McManus Kunoth relates the importance of young men being on Country, of getting out of town.



“Too much poison is what we live today, in town where you are trapped by drugs, alcohol, police, courts and the system,” he says. “We have to get young people back on Country to take care of homelands, to be self-sufficient, to not rely on government. “There’s social media and the phones are a problem. To get a young fella out of town without a phone, that phone and him is going to be the problem, to get him in a car and get him on Country, he’s going [to] want to know what his friends are doing, what his girlfriend is doing.” The glow of a campfire lures us back to a small gathering of men watching Red Dust co-ordinator Tyrone Lynch deftly cooking chops on a barbecue grill. Kunoth and Byson join the group and a yarning circle is convened to a crackling fire as the smell of barbecue meats punctuate the fragrant desert air. Red Dust Role Models on Country for a yarning circle catch up with Damien Kunoth (back to camera) and, from left, Tyrone Lynch, Chris Hagan, Dhandrey Hagan (Anmatyerr), Solomon George (Anmatyerr) and Alan Palmer. Justin McManus Kunoth leads the yarn by way of a simple reflection on the sort of day he’s had. Each participant follows suit, and all agree their day is better for getting out of town, on Country, and around a fire. Kunoth then asks the question – what would they like to change about their life if they could? Dhandrey Hagan, a young Anmatyerr man, responds by speaking about the challenges of navigating the whitefellas’ world.



“When I got to high school I experienced racism and that holds you back. It destroys your confidence, makes it harder to learn in class and that carries through to getting a job,” he says. “Confidence is a challenge, sometimes I have it, sometimes I don’t. “I feel more confident through Red Dust and activities on Country like this because they give you that opportunity to speak and share culture. They point you in the right direction, we go out help kids with the Rangers group and get them involved, teach them to look for their tucker and look after country and native animals.” Solomon George, also an Anmatyerr man, speaks of the benefits of being out bush. “Would be good to go out camping with the elders and learn stories and songlines. Living in Alice there’s nothing to do, just walk around, I make Aboriginal weapons like boomerang. Would be better out bush, visit sacred sites connect with the soul.” Solomon George takes part in the yarn circle on Country. Justin McManus There’s a sense of a longing for the old ways from these men; that the white man’s world doesn’t accept or work for them, and it’s a point of last resistance and hope to maintain culture and lore that gives them status as men. The head of the snake Regional manager Alan Palmer sits in Red Dust Role Models’ makeshift workshop where the organisation teaches mechanics and other trade skills. He uses a cultural metaphor to illustrate the plight of Aboriginal men in Alice Springs and the wider NT community – explaining their disempowerment and the consequent decline of traditional structures that have led to a breakdown in family and community responsibilities.



“If you cut the head of the snake the rest of the body is going to flounder – there’s no guidance, direction or leadership. The same thing with Indigenous people and families. In the cultural structure of Indigenous society, men play a vital role in protecting, providing, sheltering family and communities, that’s the obligation and responsibility of all Indigenous men and is embedded in our societal structures.” Red Dust’s programs seek to encourage individual responsibility for violent behaviour, dissuading men from a mindset of saying “colonisation made me do it”, or “my wife made me do it” as an excuse. They aim to be more nuanced in their approach, allowing men to express frustrations with modern and colonial society that undermine their roles in family, while emphasising the importance of traditional law taught through initiation. Alan Palmer from Red Dust Role Models. Justin McManus Alan, along with his fellow Red Dust co-ordinators Lynch and Chris Hagen, relate a sense of despair among Aboriginal men about the way they are portrayed in mainstream media, describing it as stereotypical generalisations by outsiders with little knowledge of their lives or traditional responsibilities. Palmer revisits the “head of the snake” metaphor when describing the impact of the Northern Territory Intervention in 2007 when prime minister John Howard deployed military personnel and police into Aboriginal communities in response to the Little Children are Sacred report into child sexual abuse in communities. Aboriginal men throughout the territory felt the fallout from the intervention and have struggled to regain their place to lead and govern their families and communities.



“It was a process that degraded and demoralised the head of the snake,” Palmer says. “The Northern Territory is living (the result of) its own history, the intervention is evidence of that; we are a singular population of people that was targeted to save ourselves from ourselves where our rights were taken away from us, everything our forefathers fought for was taken back. Related Article Exclusive

Indigenous ‘Sit down, talk with Indigenous Australians’: Wyatt’s message to Hanson after ‘primitive’ comments “What sort of sovereignty, autonomy, independence or self-determination can come from that. You’re looking at a population that’s in despair.” Palmer says during the intervention process, lawyers sought to reduce their clients’ sentences by claiming sexual violence was part of Aboriginal culture, a misconception that led to the demonisation of all Aboriginal men. “If the lawyers did their job they would have called it for what it was – rape and paedophilia. But sadly out of that attack on Indigenous men and Indigenous culture, (all) men got the blame for that,” Palmer says. The Northern Territory experiences an average of 61 incidents of domestic, family and sexual violence (DFSV) a day and a homicide rate of four per 100,000 people a year. Aboriginal women account for 89 per cent of these DFSV cases. The rate is more than three times that of the wider Australian community. The Domestic Family Violence Commission, in a summary report in 2025, listed the importance of Aboriginal-led responses and that Indigenous organisations and communities consistently emphasised the need for greater investment in Aboriginal community-controlled DFSV services, culturally grounded healing models and transitions to community control for women’s safe houses.

World.title: Why Marc Fennell threw himself into the ‘deep end’ of the manosphere
World.content:
CultureTV & radioAustralian TV Why Marc Fennell threw himself into the ‘deep end’ of the manosphere Nicole Elphick October 11, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Walkley Award-winning journalist Marc Fennell is going all-in with his new documentary series about the manosphere. “I mean, I get asked about my morning erections, which is pretty f---ing weird,” he says, with a laugh. “I am really chucked in the deep end. I put on the boxing gloves in a brawling pen. I get my testosterone tested. I’m knee-deep in the Enhanced Games [a controversial sporting event that allows athletes to take performance-enhancing drugs]. I fire a gun with a millionaire influencer. It’s action packed.” Marc Fennell (left) has a new documentary series all about the manosphere. ABC Fennell is an almost-omnipresent face and voice in the media landscape these days. He’s familiar to many as the host of the Australian version of quiz show Mastermind and from his stint presenting SBS current affairs show The Feed, as well as his popular podcasts No One Saw it Coming, It Burns, Nut Jobs and Stuff the British Stole – the latter of which spawned a whole TV show. His latest work, The State of Man, sees him travelling far and wide across three episodes to dive into the manosphere – the deceptively catchy name for the amorphous and destructive network of online channels and creators that promote male dominance and denigrate feminism.



“I’d been looking at it for a while, for a couple of years in fact, and I noticed that in conversations about men and masculinity online something had gotten quite darker,” Fennell says. “Everything started to metastasise around money or dominating women in relationships, and the acceptable standard of what a body was seemed to be changing.” Editor's pick Streaming The best new TV shows to stream in October He was also disturbed to see the role technology was playing in disseminating these ideas, a notion hammered home one evening when the father of two was cooking dinner for his family with YouTube on in the living room playing Minecraft and Pokemon videos. When he looked over 20 minutes later he was shocked to see the screen was now autoplaying a clip of Joe Rogan. Marc Fennell ABC



One of the key threads throughout The State of Man is how young men are funnelled into being exposed to misogynistic concepts. In a truly frightening experiment, Fennell sets up a phone with a “Young Marc” social media profile to see how long it takes the algorithm to start feeding him manosphere content. “The first week it was basically showing bicep tips. The second week, it started to get into some fairly full-on ‘you must dominate, you must pay for all your dates’ relationship stuff. Then after that, it was full-blown racist AI slop. The rules were I wasn’t allowed to click on anything, I just scrolled. The way [the algorithm] is pulling, particularly young men, in a certain direction is really horrific.” The manosphere has been having a moment in the spotlight this year. The Netflix series Louis Theroux: Inside the Manosphere saw the superstar documentarian delve into the issue, and a viral 60 Minutes interview with the looksmaxxing influencer known as Clavicular also ignited water-cooler conversation. Coming on the heels of so much coverage, Fennell feels his documentary provides a different perspective. “Look, I think what we’ve done is a much better holistic picture of the manosphere if you actually want to work out where this thing came from, who it really affects, how it can be solved – not just a bunch of cooked content creators saying and doing dumb things. If you actually want a proper picture of the manosphere, no shade on any other documentary, but I do feel like this is the best and clearest picture of the manosphere I’ve ever seen.”



Notably, Fennell speaks with not only those who have been caught up in its clutches, but also with academics who have studied it, an ex-CEO of Facebook, and even former prime minister Julia Gillard. Related Article Review What to stream this week: Louis Theroux gets inside the manosphere, plus five more picks So after all that, what was his biggest takeaway? “We can go down a different path if we want,” Fennell says. “We can change the way we raise boys, we can change the way we do adolescence, we can change the algorithm. And men in particular have to decide: are you going to be one of those guys who think the world’s out to get you and women are the enemy, or do you want to build something better?

World.title: Truths are eternal, but change is constant
World.content:
You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month.

It’s interesting to see how far back we can go when tracing still familiar sayings, such as: “In this world nothing can be said to be certain, except death and taxes.”

American statesman Benjamin Franklin popularised the saying in 1789, but is said to have quoted from a play written by Christopher Bullock in 1716. In 2026 I think I’m safe in adding a third certainty, namely “change”.

Not that change wasn’t causing concern back in Franklin’s day. Scottish Anglican cleric Henry Francis Lyte (1793-1847), who wrote the much-loved hymn Abide with Me, included the words “Change and decay in all around I see. Oh thou who changest not, abide with me.” Which raises the question: Are change and decay necessarily synonymous?

Benjamin Franklin is known for one special phrase – which he may not have coined at all. Getty Images

These days the word change is mostly preceded by “climate”. But there are many types of change surrounding us throughout our lives. Life stages themselves bring necessary and potentially rewarding changes. Growing up, seeking our vocation, discovering our sexuality, each generates and demands change. Loss of employment, relationship breakdown and the deaths of loved ones over the years can easily derail.

World.title: Helicopters, military door knocks and 9pm curfews: Five years since Sydney’s dystopian divide
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

There was a moment in western Sydney, just over five years ago, when it felt like the world had collapsed. It struck people at different times. To some, it was when they heard the whirr of police helicopters demanding people return home. To others, it was the sight of officers patrolling empty streets on horseback. Others felt the apocalypse in seeing the military doorknock residents in Granville, or hearing of people fined for leaving their suburbs. This was western Sydney during the 2021 lockdown: a whirlwind of death, a storm of disease and economic collapse leaving nothing behind. Sunday will mark exactly half a decade since the restrictions were lifted after they throttled the region and left nothing the same. To Boraa Dannoun, the realisation that his world had been upended came as he was organising a Zoom funeral for his father, only days after he had buried his mother. Both of his parents died of COVID in the final week of the 2021 lockdowns, buried just as the restrictions were lifted. Boraa Dannoun at Rookwood cemetery visiting the graves of his parents, both of whom he lost during the COVID lockdown of 2021. Sitthixay Ditthavong “They died so quickly, and in such quick succession that there was no time to prepare ourselves,” he said. “The core of the family was shattered. You cannot go through the stages of grief as you normally would. I felt numb, in denial. “Because of the restrictions, nobody could give condolences in person. We were prevented from saying farewell on our terms – even how we said goodbye was controlled, making the most sacred moment of our lives feel entirely impersonal and surreal.”



The courier driver, who was living in Punchbowl at the time, remembers the worst week of his life in excruciating detail. He remembers each parent’s final words to him, the late-night dashes to different hospitals, the confusion and the sinking, crushing helplessness. Restrictive grief Between June and October 2021, 374 people died of COVID in NSW. The 12 “LGAs of concern”, which included Bayside, Blacktown, Burwood, Campbelltown, Canterbury-Bankstown, Cumberland, Fairfield, Georges River, Liverpool, Parramatta, Strathfield and Penrith, had the highest number of cases across the four-month stretch. From late August 2021, residents in those LGAs were banned from going outside from 9pm to 5am, and were restricted to a 5km radius for grocery shopping and exercise. They were only allowed out of their homes for one hour a day. A man in Bexley, within an LGA of concern, looks out of his apartment in August 2021, when residents could only leave home for food or other goods, or exercise. Kate Geraghty These restrictions were also heavily policed; the NSW Bureau of Crime Statistics and Research in 2021 found police disproportionately fined residents from those western Sydney LGAs, with the bureau finding no evidence of “non-compliant activities” in the region. It was amid those restrictions that Mike Searle had to eulogise his grandmother via video, with none of his family to grieve with him.



“I was probably closest to her more than anyone else in the world,” he said. “And we’re sitting there, and I’m watching myself eulogise my grandmother with my ‘bubble buddy’, with her little certificate that allowed her to be there. Mike Searle at his home in Rhodes. During lockdown, Searle had to eulogise his grandmother via video, with none of his family to grieve with him. Oscar Colman “It just felt very dystopian.” He felt permanently changed by the ordeal. “I think it has changed my philosophy on shared grief,” he said. “I feel like my grief was prolonged, and that I was sad for a lot longer than I needed to be. “Because what I missed was that kind of shared communal grieving process. “Not being with my family or my friends to work through those five stages of grief just made it a lot harder.”



A political awakening From her office in the heart of Fairfield, one of the first epicentres of the 2021 outbreaks that led to the restrictions, Tairyn Vergara worked tirelessly to organise food and supplies for the families doing it tough. The chief executive officer of The Parks Community Network witnessed a rising resentment around her, as the bite of the lockdowns led into the crunch of the cost-of-living crisis. “I think people felt that it wasn’t handled fairly, that it was easier to be tougher with some people than others, and I think that probably has stayed with us all this time,” she said. “And now, that resentment has turned to anger.” Rents, grocery prices, bills, interest rates and services have all increased exponentially alongside stagnating salaries across the country. In western Sydney, the crisis has left many with the same issues they faced during lockdown. To Vergara, both the lockdowns and the economic crisis that followed have folded into each other, combining to fuel outrage at governments of every level. Tairyn Vergara, chief executive of the Parks Community Network, says there is still anger about the COVID lockdowns. Sitthixay Ditthavong



Dannoun, who still grieves his parents every day, said his experience ultimately left him with questions about how his family’s ordeal was managed, which have morphed into a broader political scepticism. “The government COVID protocols have made me incredibly sceptical of politicians and the NSW health system,” he said. “I don’t believe everything was done to save my parents.” His scepticism is rooted in concerns shared by many in the region about the decision to issue severe public health orders that only applied to western Sydney; a sense that you are treated differently based on your postcode. One particular moment that seemed to encapsulate that feeling: Bondi Beach packed with maskless picnickers while people in western Sydney could barely leave their homes. “I don’t think anyone has really forgotten, that sort of trauma doesn’t go away in five years,” said Adam Leto, head of the Western Sydney Leadership Dialogue. Leto was a recurring figure during the lockdowns, speaking incessantly on the issues and challenges faced by western Sydney. “People couldn’t go outside for a walk,” he said. “They couldn’t see and care for their loved ones or friends. They couldn’t go to work. And that breeds a fair bit of anger, that was intensified when they turned on their TVs to see people in Bondi having picnics on the beach.” In Sydney’s eastern suburbs, residents were free to visit Bondi Beach if they lived within the 5km radius in 2021. Steven Siewert

World.title: ‘Time for a new president’: Trump calls on Zelensky to go amid diesel stoush
World.content:
Breaking WorldNorth AmericaRussia-Ukraine war ‘Time for a new president’: Trump calls on Zelensky to go amid diesel stoush Michael Koziol Updated October 11, 2026 — 6:22am ,first published 5:22am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Washington: Donald Trump said Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky “better damn well stop” striking Russia’s diesel refineries and called for the wartime leader to leave office, as relations between the two sink to fresh lows over skyrocketing diesel prices. The US president on Friday struck a deal to buy Russian diesel, upending years of sanctions against Moscow, though it was not evident that Vladimir Putin could fulfil his end of the deal, given he is struggling to fuel his own economy. Donald Trump said it was time for Ukraine to get a new president as he condemned Zelensky for striking Russia’s diesel refineries. AP Photo/Nathan Howard On Saturday (US time), Trump again lashed out at Zelensky, blaming him for the ongoing war that was started by Russia, and calling for him to be replaced as president. “Zelensky could have settled this war many times - many, many times. He chooses not to. Very difficult,” Trump told reporters while leaving the White House for a rally on Tennessee.



“We said you can do whatever you want to Russia, don’t hit the refineries because that’s a world problem that’s caused. He wants to make problems for the world, he wants to make problems for our farmers, our ranchers.” Ukraine has pummelled Russian energy infrastructure in an attempt to cripple Putin’s economy and deprive Moscow of funding for the war. Russia has imposed a diesel export ban as it battles to fuel its own needs. Ukraine has stepped up its long-range bombardment of the Moscow region, including oil refineries like this one, on Sunday. AP But the diesel shortage has flowed through the world economy and contributed to rising prices in the US just weeks before the midterm elections, in which energy costs – primarily petrol prices – are a major issue for American consumers, farmers and industry. Trump has repeatedly called on Zelensky to halt strikes against Russia’s energy infrastructure.



“We told him ‘do whatever you want but don’t hit the diesel fuel’ … and what does he do, he goes and hits the diesel fuel. He can do whatever he wants, but he can’t do that,” Trump said Saturday. Related Article Russia-Ukraine war Natalie’s brother went missing within a year of signing up. She still doesn’t know where he is “He’s not going to affect our farmers, and he’s not going to affect our ranchers, and he’s not going to affect the rest of the world. He better damn well stop.” The US president then went further, calling for Zelensky to go. “You know what I suggest? I suggest they get a new leader who can make a deal. He could have made many deals and for some reason he never does. “That’s a war that should have never started, and I think it’s time for Ukraine to get a new president.”



The comments represent arguably the lowest point in relations between Trump and Zelensky since the infamous Oval Office meeting in late February last year, early in Trump’s second term, when Vice President JD Vance said Zelensky was ungrateful for US support. The leaders raised their voices at each other, and the encounter ended with Zelensky being forced to depart the White House early. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky (left) and British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband (second from right) at the site of a deadly attack in Pryluky on Thursday. Ukrainian Presidential Press Office via AP While relations improved later, Trump has routinely blamed the Ukrainian president for either starting the war - which began when Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine - or failing to accept a deal to end the conflict. Such deals would have involved Ukraine ceding significant amounts of territory to Russia, even land that was not fully occupied by Russian forces.



Zelensky has shied away from directly criticising Trump since that tempestuous Oval Office meeting, but on Friday he called the diesel deal “weak” and unfair, and a birthday gift to Putin. On Saturday, 20 people, including three children, were killed in a Russian attack on the southern Ukrainian city of Zaporizhzhia. It has been a regular target of Russian bombardment, with strikes intensifying in the past few months. Workers extinguish a fire after a Russian drone strike in Zaporizhzhia, Ukraine. AP Photo/Kateryna Klochko A 6-year-old girl was among those killed when one strike reduced part of an apartment block to rubble. Her grandfather, Anatoliy Chumniy, stood sobbing over her body, laid on the ground ​in a white bag, after rescuers pulled it from the wreckage.“Her birthday would have been at the end of the month,” he said through tears. Zelensky said the strikes on Zaporizhzhia were a “thank you” for the lifting of ‌sanctions on diesel exports.



Related Article Analysis

Trump diplomacy Trump promised to end the Russia-Ukraine war in a day. Now he’s funding it As anger brewed among Republicans about Trump’s diesel deal with Putin, former vice president Mike Pence said the decision made “no sense” and betrayed the legacy of the late Republican senator Lindsey Graham, who fought for fresh sanctions on Russia and its trading partners before his sudden death in July. “Putin is losing this war,” Pence said. “Ukraine has fought the Russian military to a standstill and reinvented warfare with drones taking the fight into the heart of Russia. “America should not be throwing a lifeline to Putin’s war machine. Now is the time to stand strong against Russian aggression as we did during the first Trump administration.” With Reuters Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: Songlines, ceremony and small steps: The search for hope among the men of Alice Springs
World.content:
Amid intense scrutiny over family violence, local leaders and elders are getting young Indigenous men back on Country to reclaim culture and responsibilities.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

After days of dreary rain following Kumanjayi Little Baby’s funeral, the veil of grief and Sorry Business eases over Alice Springs. The men at Red Dust Role Models, a non-profit mentoring organisation for Indigenous people, have organised an impromptu gathering in the foothills of the East MacDonnell ranges – Country of the Black Caterpillar dreaming, Tyape Utnerrengatye. Red Dust, along with community leaders and local men, have sought to give this masthead an understanding of the plight of men in Alice Springs, and the wider central desert region. To explore the complexity of issues that lead to, but do not excuse, the extreme rates of domestic, family and sexual violence in the community. Now they are on Country, amid a stunning and monumental landscape. The Black Caterpillar Dreaming story of the ranges stretches out along the landscape to beyond the horizon, adorned in vibrant hues of red, pink and yellow desert blooms and vivid green tussock grass after the rain. Traditional owner Damien Kunoth arrives early with his son Byson. The men walk the land in the way of their ancestors, along songlines, acknowledging sacred sites and searching for food; for bush banana (upali) and bush coconut (kandar), which are in abundance, but past their best. Traditional owner Damien Kunoth (Arrernte) with son Byson on country outside Alice Springs. Justin McManus Kunoth relates the importance of young men being on Country, of getting out of town.



“Too much poison is what we live today, in town where you are trapped by drugs, alcohol, police, courts and the system,” he says. “We have to get young people back on Country to take care of homelands, to be self-sufficient, to not rely on government. “There’s social media and the phones are a problem. To get a young fella out of town without a phone, that phone and him is going to be the problem, to get him in a car and get him on Country, he’s going [to] want to know what his friends are doing, what his girlfriend is doing.” The glow of a campfire lures us back to a small gathering of men watching Red Dust co-ordinator Tyrone Lynch deftly cooking chops on a barbecue grill. Kunoth and Byson join the group and a yarning circle is convened to a crackling fire as the smell of barbecue meats punctuate the fragrant desert air. Red Dust Role Models on Country for a yarning circle catch up with Damien Kunoth (back to camera) and, from left, Tyrone Lynch, Chris Hagan, Dhandrey Hagan (Anmatyerr), Solomon George (Anmatyerr) and Alan Palmer. Justin McManus Kunoth leads the yarn by way of a simple reflection on the sort of day he’s had. Each participant follows suit, and all agree their day is better for getting out of town, on Country, and around a fire. Kunoth then asks the question – what would they like to change about their life if they could? Dhandrey Hagan, a young Anmatyerr man, responds by speaking about the challenges of navigating the whitefellas’ world.



“When I got to high school I experienced racism and that holds you back. It destroys your confidence, makes it harder to learn in class and that carries through to getting a job,” he says. “Confidence is a challenge, sometimes I have it, sometimes I don’t. “I feel more confident through Red Dust and activities on Country like this because they give you that opportunity to speak and share culture. They point you in the right direction, we go out help kids with the Rangers group and get them involved, teach them to look for their tucker and look after country and native animals.” Solomon George, also an Anmatyerr man, speaks of the benefits of being out bush. “Would be good to go out camping with the elders and learn stories and songlines. Living in Alice there’s nothing to do, just walk around, I make Aboriginal weapons like boomerang. Would be better out bush, visit sacred sites connect with the soul.” Solomon George takes part in the yarn circle on Country. Justin McManus There’s a sense of a longing for the old ways from these men; that the white man’s world doesn’t accept or work for them, and it’s a point of last resistance and hope to maintain culture and lore that gives them status as men. The head of the snake Regional manager Alan Palmer sits in Red Dust Role Models’ makeshift workshop where the organisation teaches mechanics and other trade skills. He uses a cultural metaphor to illustrate the plight of Aboriginal men in Alice Springs and the wider NT community – explaining their disempowerment and the consequent decline of traditional structures that have led to a breakdown in family and community responsibilities.



“If you cut the head of the snake the rest of the body is going to flounder – there’s no guidance, direction or leadership. The same thing with Indigenous people and families. In the cultural structure of Indigenous society, men play a vital role in protecting, providing, sheltering family and communities, that’s the obligation and responsibility of all Indigenous men and is embedded in our societal structures.” Red Dust’s programs seek to encourage individual responsibility for violent behaviour, dissuading men from a mindset of saying “colonisation made me do it”, or “my wife made me do it” as an excuse. They aim to be more nuanced in their approach, allowing men to express frustrations with modern and colonial society that undermine their roles in family, while emphasising the importance of traditional law taught through initiation. Alan Palmer from Red Dust Role Models. Justin McManus Alan, along with his fellow Red Dust co-ordinators Lynch and Chris Hagen, relate a sense of despair among Aboriginal men about the way they are portrayed in mainstream media, describing it as stereotypical generalisations by outsiders with little knowledge of their lives or traditional responsibilities. Palmer revisits the “head of the snake” metaphor when describing the impact of the Northern Territory Intervention in 2007 when prime minister John Howard deployed military personnel and police into Aboriginal communities in response to the Little Children are Sacred report into child sexual abuse in communities. Aboriginal men throughout the territory felt the fallout from the intervention and have struggled to regain their place to lead and govern their families and communities.



“It was a process that degraded and demoralised the head of the snake,” Palmer says. “The Northern Territory is living (the result of) its own history, the intervention is evidence of that; we are a singular population of people that was targeted to save ourselves from ourselves where our rights were taken away from us, everything our forefathers fought for was taken back. Related Article Exclusive

Indigenous ‘Sit down, talk with Indigenous Australians’: Wyatt’s message to Hanson after ‘primitive’ comments “What sort of sovereignty, autonomy, independence or self-determination can come from that. You’re looking at a population that’s in despair.” Palmer says during the intervention process, lawyers sought to reduce their clients’ sentences by claiming sexual violence was part of Aboriginal culture, a misconception that led to the demonisation of all Aboriginal men. “If the lawyers did their job they would have called it for what it was – rape and paedophilia. But sadly out of that attack on Indigenous men and Indigenous culture, (all) men got the blame for that,” Palmer says. The Northern Territory experiences an average of 61 incidents of domestic, family and sexual violence (DFSV) a day and a homicide rate of four per 100,000 people a year. Aboriginal women account for 89 per cent of these DFSV cases. The rate is more than three times that of the wider Australian community. The Domestic Family Violence Commission, in a summary report in 2025, listed the importance of Aboriginal-led responses and that Indigenous organisations and communities consistently emphasised the need for greater investment in Aboriginal community-controlled DFSV services, culturally grounded healing models and transitions to community control for women’s safe houses.

World.title: Why Marc Fennell threw himself into the ‘deep end’ of the manosphere
World.content:
CultureTV & radioAustralian TV Why Marc Fennell threw himself into the ‘deep end’ of the manosphere Nicole Elphick October 11, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Walkley Award-winning journalist Marc Fennell is going all-in with his new documentary series about the manosphere. “I mean, I get asked about my morning erections, which is pretty f---ing weird,” he says, with a laugh. “I am really chucked in the deep end. I put on the boxing gloves in a brawling pen. I get my testosterone tested. I’m knee-deep in the Enhanced Games [a controversial sporting event that allows athletes to take performance-enhancing drugs]. I fire a gun with a millionaire influencer. It’s action packed.” Marc Fennell (left) has a new documentary series all about the manosphere. ABC Fennell is an almost-omnipresent face and voice in the media landscape these days. He’s familiar to many as the host of the Australian version of quiz show Mastermind and from his stint presenting SBS current affairs show The Feed, as well as his popular podcasts No One Saw it Coming, It Burns, Nut Jobs and Stuff the British Stole – the latter of which spawned a whole TV show. His latest work, The State of Man, sees him travelling far and wide across three episodes to dive into the manosphere – the deceptively catchy name for the amorphous and destructive network of online channels and creators that promote male dominance and denigrate feminism.



“I’d been looking at it for a while, for a couple of years in fact, and I noticed that in conversations about men and masculinity online something had gotten quite darker,” Fennell says. “Everything started to metastasise around money or dominating women in relationships, and the acceptable standard of what a body was seemed to be changing.” Editor's pick Streaming The best new TV shows to stream in October He was also disturbed to see the role technology was playing in disseminating these ideas, a notion hammered home one evening when the father of two was cooking dinner for his family with YouTube on in the living room playing Minecraft and Pokemon videos. When he looked over 20 minutes later he was shocked to see the screen was now autoplaying a clip of Joe Rogan. Marc Fennell ABC



One of the key threads throughout The State of Man is how young men are funnelled into being exposed to misogynistic concepts. In a truly frightening experiment, Fennell sets up a phone with a “Young Marc” social media profile to see how long it takes the algorithm to start feeding him manosphere content. “The first week it was basically showing bicep tips. The second week, it started to get into some fairly full-on ‘you must dominate, you must pay for all your dates’ relationship stuff. Then after that, it was full-blown racist AI slop. The rules were I wasn’t allowed to click on anything, I just scrolled. The way [the algorithm] is pulling, particularly young men, in a certain direction is really horrific.” The manosphere has been having a moment in the spotlight this year. The Netflix series Louis Theroux: Inside the Manosphere saw the superstar documentarian delve into the issue, and a viral 60 Minutes interview with the looksmaxxing influencer known as Clavicular also ignited water-cooler conversation. Coming on the heels of so much coverage, Fennell feels his documentary provides a different perspective. “Look, I think what we’ve done is a much better holistic picture of the manosphere if you actually want to work out where this thing came from, who it really affects, how it can be solved – not just a bunch of cooked content creators saying and doing dumb things. If you actually want a proper picture of the manosphere, no shade on any other documentary, but I do feel like this is the best and clearest picture of the manosphere I’ve ever seen.”



Notably, Fennell speaks with not only those who have been caught up in its clutches, but also with academics who have studied it, an ex-CEO of Facebook, and even former prime minister Julia Gillard. Related Article Review What to stream this week: Louis Theroux gets inside the manosphere, plus five more picks So after all that, what was his biggest takeaway? “We can go down a different path if we want,” Fennell says. “We can change the way we raise boys, we can change the way we do adolescence, we can change the algorithm. And men in particular have to decide: are you going to be one of those guys who think the world’s out to get you and women are the enemy, or do you want to build something better?

World.title: Truths are eternal, but change is constant
World.content:
You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month.

It’s interesting to see how far back we can go when tracing still familiar sayings, such as: “In this world nothing can be said to be certain, except death and taxes.”

American statesman Benjamin Franklin popularised the saying in 1789, but is said to have quoted from a play written by Christopher Bullock in 1716. In 2026 I think I’m safe in adding a third certainty, namely “change”.

Not that change wasn’t causing concern back in Franklin’s day. Scottish Anglican cleric Henry Francis Lyte (1793-1847), who wrote the much-loved hymn Abide with Me, included the words “Change and decay in all around I see. Oh thou who changest not, abide with me.” Which raises the question: Are change and decay necessarily synonymous?

Benjamin Franklin is known for one special phrase – which he may not have coined at all. Getty Images

These days the word change is mostly preceded by “climate”. But there are many types of change surrounding us throughout our lives. Life stages themselves bring necessary and potentially rewarding changes. Growing up, seeking our vocation, discovering our sexuality, each generates and demands change. Loss of employment, relationship breakdown and the deaths of loved ones over the years can easily derail.

There was a moment in western Sydney, just over five years ago, when it felt like the world had collapsed. It struck people at different times. To some, it was when they heard the whirr of police helicopters demanding people return home. To others, it was the sight of officers patrolling empty streets on horseback. Both of his parents died of COVID in the final week of the 2021 lockdowns, buried just as the restrictions were lifted. Boraa Dannoun at Rookwood cemetery visiting the graves of his parents, both of whom he lost during the COVID lockdown of 2021. Sitthixay Ditthavong “They died so quickly, and in such quick succession that there was no time to prepare ourselves,” he said. “The core of the family was shattered. The courier driver, who was living in Punchbowl at the time, remembers the worst week of his life in excruciating detail. He remembers each parent’s final words to him, the late-night dashes to different hospitals, the confusion and the sinking, crushing helplessness. Restrictive grief Between June and October 2021, 374 people died of COVID in NSW. The 12 “LGAs of concern”, which included Bayside, Blacktown, Burwood, Campbelltown, Canterbury-Bankstown, Cumberland, Fairfield, Georges River, Liverpool, Parramatta, Strathfield and Penrith, had the highest number of cases across the four-month stretch. From late August 2021, residents in those LGAs were banned from going outside from 9pm to 5am, and were restricted to a 5km radius for grocery shopping and exercise. They were only allowed out of their homes for one hour a day. A man in Bexley, within an LGA of concern, looks out of his apartment in August 2021, when residents could only leave home for food or other goods, or exercise. Kate Geraghty These restrictions were also heavily policed; the NSW Bureau of Crime Statistics and Research in 2021 found police disproportionately fined residents from those western Sydney LGAs, with the bureau finding no evidence of “non-compliant activities” in the region. It was amid those restrictions that Mike Searle had to eulogise his grandmother via video, with none of his family to grieve with him.



“I was probably closest to her more than anyone else in the world,” he said. “And we’re sitting there, and I’m watching myself eulogise my grandmother with my ‘bubble buddy’, with her little certificate that allowed her to be there. Mike Searle at his home in Rhodes. During lockdown, Searle had to eulogise his grandmother via video, with none of his family to grieve with him. Oscar Colman “It just felt very dystopian.” He felt permanently changed by the ordeal. “I think it has changed my philosophy on shared grief,” he said. “I feel like my grief was prolonged, and that I was sad for a lot longer than I needed to be. “Because what I missed was that kind of shared communal grieving process. “Not being with my family or my friends to work through those five stages of grief just made it a lot harder.”



A political awakening From her office in the heart of Fairfield, one of the first epicentres of the 2021 outbreaks that led to the restrictions, Tairyn Vergara worked tirelessly to organise food and supplies for the families doing it tough. The chief executive officer of The Parks Community Network witnessed a rising resentment around her, as the bite of the lockdowns led into the crunch of the cost-of-living crisis. “I think people felt that it wasn’t handled fairly, that it was easier to be tougher with some people than others, and I think that probably has stayed with us all this time,” she said. “And now, that resentment has turned to anger.” Rents, grocery prices, bills, interest rates and services have all increased exponentially alongside stagnating salaries across the country. In western Sydney, the crisis has left many with the same issues they faced during lockdown. To Vergara, both the lockdowns and the economic crisis that followed have folded into each other, combining to fuel outrage at governments of every level. Tairyn Vergara, chief executive of the Parks Community Network, says there is still anger about the COVID lockdowns. Sitthixay Ditthavong



Dannoun, who still grieves his parents every day, said his experience ultimately left him with questions about how his family’s ordeal was managed, which have morphed into a broader political scepticism. “The government COVID protocols have made me incredibly sceptical of politicians and the NSW health system,” he said. “I don’t believe everything was done to save my parents.” His scepticism is rooted in concerns shared by many in the region about the decision to issue severe public health orders that only applied to western Sydney; a sense that you are treated differently based on your postcode. One particular moment that seemed to encapsulate that feeling: Bondi Beach packed with maskless picnickers while people in western Sydney could barely leave their homes. “I don’t think anyone has really forgotten, that sort of trauma doesn’t go away in five years,” said Adam Leto, head of the Western Sydney Leadership Dialogue. Leto was a recurring figure during the lockdowns, speaking incessantly on the issues and challenges faced by western Sydney. “People couldn’t go outside for a walk,” he said. “They couldn’t see and care for their loved ones or friends. They couldn’t go to work. And that breeds a fair bit of anger, that was intensified when they turned on their TVs to see people in Bondi having picnics on the beach.” In Sydney’s eastern suburbs, residents were free to visit Bondi Beach if they lived within the 5km radius in 2021. Steven Siewert

World.title: The ‘glass skin’ Korean beauty trend has risks, experts warn
World.content: The glass skin trend has its roots in South Korean beauty culture, where the term is used to describe a complexion that appears exceptionally smooth and pore-less. The phrase appears to have first come around in the early to mid-2010s and then saw a major spike at the end of 2025 going into 2026, according to Google trends. Those who subscribe to the complex routines say their skin benefits from the layers of hydration, and viewers are hooked on the ASMR-like videos as influencers tap their glass-like faces with their fingers and beauty tools.

World.title: Auckland Council using discounts to separate trash and treasure at transfer station
World.content:
People taking unwanted household items to an Auckland resource recovery park are getting a discount for sorting their waste.

The initiative at Waitakere Resource Recovery Park created employment and diverted waste, Auckland Council refuse manager Dick Fong said.

The council has an aspirational goal of zero waste by 2040, but Fong said it was a challenge to improve waste diversion without employing additional staff, so the discount was introduced to encourage people to change their behaviour.

"They love the discount, but they also love the fact that they're actually doing something that's actually helping save resources.

"We've had a bit of feedback that people are happy to do this sorting without a discount, but we're happy to give it to create that good behavior change."

A 10 percent discount trialled last year was increased to 15 percent in July.

People taking unwanted items to Waitākere Resource Recovery Park receive a discount when they sort their waste into marked bins. Auckland Council

Fong said this year a new unloading area had made it easier for customers to separate their waste into bins for products such as wood, steel, cardboard, plastics, and refuse.

There was also a hazardous waste drop-off area, he said.

Any good, reusable materials were sold in a recycle shop on site run by community group McLaren Park Henderson South Community Trust, he said.

Fong said there was always a volume of waste that could not be reused.

"That's the component that we're actually separating and finding markets for and getting them taken out of landfill.

World.title: The All Blacks dominated the Wallabies. Their struggle in South Africa made it possible
World.content:
It appears the All Blacks did learn a thing or two in South Africa after all - their 50-19 victory over the Wallabies at Eden Park on Saturday night which allowed them to retain the Bledisloe Cup for another year contained all sorts of improvements, most notably their ability to catch a high ball.

Their aerial prowess was just one aspect of a victory which helped them break a three-test losing streak and take their unbeaten record at their fortress to 54 tests.

Their ability to finish opportunities - a major issue in South Africa - was also vastly improved.

They scored seven tries to Australia's three and may have scored one or two more had Will Jordan not looked to create opportunities for others rather than seek them himself. Naturally, he made the most of a very late one to put an exclamation mark on the win.

A rare try for replacement prop Pasilio Tosi was also scrubbed out for an earlier knock-on.

So, the drought for the poor old Aussies goes on - they lost the big trophy in 2003 and have not held it since - and, while they were in this test at halftime with the score 17-14 to the home side, they were blown away in the second half.

They could not deal with the speed of thought and action of men such as Damian McKenzie, who looked sharp at No.10, or the almost supernatural workrate of Jordie Barrett, the man outside him in the No.12 jersey.

Tupou Vaa'i scores against Australia at Eden Park. www.photosport.nz

Barrett was everywhere, with his midfield partner Quinn Tupaea not far behind, and, with Leroy Carter and Barrett having a vastly improved night under the high ball, the All Blacks got all the possession they needed and more.

Former skipper Scott Barrett got through a mountain of work and loose forwards Peter Lakai, Tupou Vaa'i and Wallace Sititi had the better of their vaunted opposites.

There were still issues, of course.

The All Blacks' lineout maul defence began shakily, and it was a big reason for Tom Wright's early converted try, but the response was impressive and built on a lightning quick ball against which the Wallabies had no answer.

The two tries in just over two minutes for Lakai and fellow loose forward Vaa'i were based both on lightning-fast ruck speed and the All Blacks' aerial superiority.

Jordie Barrett snaffled the first for the attack set alight by McKenzie and finished nicely by Lakai and there was another high ball win before the little No.10 cut capers again for Vaa'i's try.

At 14-7 up, the All Blacks had well and truly wrested momentum away from the visitors who needed to do something to slow the opposition's ball and succeeded only in giving away penalties.

All Blacks halfback Cam Roigard celebrates his try. Brett Phibbs / www.photosport.nz

McKenzie kicked the second one to push the All Blacks out to a 17-7 lead but back came the Wallabies through skipper Harry Wilson, the big No.8 scoring under the posts after the home side's defence was caught short up the middle.

It created an unsatisfactory end to the first half for the All Blacks, who passed with accuracy in the excellent conditions and looked like dynamite when attacking from depth (as did the Wallabies), but who too often misfired at lineout time.

It was end to end stuff early in the second half with Beauden Barrett twice getting into good positions to save the All Blacks.

Jordan was again probably overly generous in trying to pass to the supporting Sititi only to see it intercepted, but the pressure stayed on the Wallabies and Cam Roigard was the beneficiary from close range.

Tries for Codie Taylor, Leroy Carter and replacement outside back Josh Moorby followed as the score got into ugly territory for the Australians.

The defeat broke a six-game unbeaten streak for the Wallabies who arrived in Auckland confident of making history after their recent victory over a weakened Springboks but they came up against an All Black team determined to right a few wrongs.

They did it in style.

All Blacks 50 (Peter Lakai, Tupou Vaa'i, Cam Roigard, Codie Taylor, Leroy Carter, Josh Moorby, Will Jordan tries; Damian McKenzie 6 cons, pen)

Australia 19 (Tom Wright, Harry Wilson, Josh Nasser tries; Ryan Lonergan 2 cons)

World.title: Opponents label National's fishing policy 'desperate' and a 'flip-flop'
World.content:
New Zealand First says National's fishing policy is desperate and unresearched, and would have huge impacts on employment and the costs of fish.

Meanwhile, environmental groups and parties to National's left say National cannot be trusted on the issue, given the party's track record this term.

After a spearfishing trip departing from Auckland's Takapuna Beach on Saturday, National leader Christopher Luxon announced the policy to ban ring-net fishing in the Hauraki Gulf, establish a new Waiheke Island marine reserve, ban commercial sales of marlin, and review bottom trawling on sea mounts with a view to reducing use of the technique over time.

'Desperate and unresearched' - Peters

NZ First's Shane Jones has been championing the fishing industry this term of government, so the policy would appear to be a shot across his bow - and Luxon said he did not care what Jones might think of it.

NZ First leader Winston Peters, after what he said was a "wall to wall" public meeting in Invercargill, suggested the consequences had not been thought through.

"It's rather desperate and it's rather unresearched as to the consequences of what they propose to do, both with respect to the workers and the fishermen and fisherwomen, and everybody's involved in the market, but also the customers and the cost of fish going forward," Peters said.

"I don't understand why he's actually making that announcement because there's been a lot of work and a lot of research going into the total consequences of such decisions, and it's premature to arrive at that because the work in its totality hasn't been done."

However, he would not commit to opposing the policy in coalition negotiations.

"Look, we just heard about it today so we're not going to rush to judgement on it, but ... when you're forced to check out what you've just heard - to its authenticity and its veracity, and its utility and its workability - it's not going to survive that test.

"We'd be opposed to it but we need the time to work on that - but I was actually quite surprised that they would make such a premature announcement."

He said the policy went against what the government had been trying to do over the past term.

"We've tried to keep in mind two things: there are thousands of workers involved, and there are also hundreds of thousands of customers involved - and within a cost of living crisis like we have, those sorts of costs are significant."

'Really disappointing' - Forest and Bird

Forest and Bird spokesperson Bianca Ranson said Labour and the Greens had offered support to National on a ring-net ban for Hauraki, so there was "no need to compromise those high protection areas by allowing fishing in them".

She said the Waiheke Marine Reserve proposal had been "sitting on their desk" for nearly two years, and the decision could have been made already.

"It's great to see some energy around protection for the gulf, but it is very much a case of why did they not act on it this term?"

National seemed to be using the issue's popularity to score points, she said.

"It's very clear that bottom trawling on the Hauraki Gulf is an election issue, we've been campaigning hard on it. There's overwhelming social licence; people want to see action in the gulf ... what has been announced today could have been done this term. It feels quite unfair to hear they're announcing these things when they've literally had the power to be able to enact them."

National can't be trusted on oceans policy - Labour, Greens

Labour leader Chris Hipkins said National's time in government suggested it would do the opposite of what it campaigned on, and the party could not be trusted.

"When we announced protections around the Hauraki Gulf when we were in government, the National Party said that they didn't go far enough and they supported them, and then in government, undid much of the work that we were doing."

Hipkins said Labour was committed to banning bottom trawling in the Hauraki Gulf, but in terms of scaling up a ban in New Zealand's EEZ, there was more work to do.

"It can't be done immediately. There's a need for us still to fish. There's jobs associated with that. As new technology emerges, and we've invested as a country in quite a lot of research and development in this area, we need to do more of that so that we can work out how to do fishing more sustainably and with less environmental impact."

Greens co-leader Chlöe Swarbrick also said the policy showed National could not be trusted on oceans policy.

"When we were going through the amendment to the Hauraki Gulf Marine Park Act ... we ended up with a proposal for these high protection areas, and then at the 11th hour ministers of this government had a backroom meeting and decided to create carve-outs in those so-called high protection areas to allow ring-net commercial fishers to continue fishing.

"Now they're turning around, understanding how deeply unpopular this is and saying they're going to campaign on undoing it. You cannot trust the National Party when it comes to conservation."

Opportunity Party welcomes shift

The Opportunity Party also noted much of the policy could have been progressed in the last three years, but welcomed the new approach.

Oceans and fisheries spokesperson Kayla Kingdon-Bebb said National did not need to rely on New Zealand First in the first place to get the legislation that created the high protection areas - including the exemptions - over the line.

"Parties on the other side of the House would have supported it. There was absolutely no need to exempt commercial fishing from those two areas in the first place. So I think it's pretty interesting to see that National's now campaigning on reversing a decision it didn't actually have to make in the last term."

One of Opportunity's five bottom lines is an immediate end to bottom trawling in inshore areas such as the Hauraki Gulf, followed by a complete phase-out.

Leader Qiulae Wong said National had "clearly been led astray by some of their coalition partners" this term and wanted to see the party go further.

World.title: Youth homelessness a 'growing reality' as Aotearoa marks World Homeless Day
World.content:
Youth homelessness is "getting younger", with support workers warning more rangatahi are going without basic necessities and safe places to stay.

Rangatahi, youth advocates and housing providers gathered in West Auckland on Saturday to mark World Homeless Day, calling for better support for young people experiencing homelessness.

The event was organised by Manaaki Rangatahi, a kaupapa Māori-led collective working to address youth housing insecurity and homelessness in Aotearoa.

Te Kou o Rehua Panapa, from Mā Te Huruhuru Charitable Trust, works with the organisation's Manukura outreach team, connecting with taitamariki experiencing homelessness across Tāmaki Makaurau.

He said the situation was changing, with younger children increasingly needing support. The night before the event, his team had connected with a 12-year-old who had been homeless for more than nine months.

"I've not seen homelessness like this before. It's a different homelessness now. It's getting younger.

"The need is more, and there's not a hell of a lot of support out there for them."

He said many young people lacked access to basic necessities, while the proportion of rangatahi Māori and Pacific young people experiencing homelessness was particularly concerning.

"I would say 90 percent are of Māori whakapapa or are from Te Moana-nui-a-Kiwa," he said.

"It hurts. It shouldn't be a reality for us as people of the land, as tangata whenua. We shouldn't be experiencing this.

"It is really hard to swallow sometimes to see our own people out there."

Te Kou o Rehua Panapa says homeless youth are getting younger and needing more support. RNZ / Coco Lance

Mā Te Huruhuru's Manukura outreach vehicle, or 'waka', allows kaimahi to go directly to young people rather than requiring them to find their way to a service.

The team provides food, hygiene products, phone-charging equipment and a safe space for rangatahi to sit down and talk.

Raising awareness was an important first step towards finding lasting solutions, Panapa said.

"We need to normalise the conversation and have more kōrero, and work collectively to come up with sustainable solutions for our taitamariki and our whānau who are currently homeless."

As Aotearoa marks World Homeless Day, Panapa wants New Zealanders to understand that homelessness and youth homeless is "a reality".

"Homelessness is not our future. It should not be our future, for our taitamariki, for our mokopuna and for our whānau."

Te Aroha Humarie Morgan-Neal, 18, says finding support helped her work towards a safer future for herself and her baby Kaos. RNZ / Coco Lance

'Change can happen'

18-year-old Te Aroha Humarie Morgan-Neal knows what it is like to experience homelessness and the importance of having somewhere safe to turn.

Morgan-Neal said she experienced "deep addiction" and an abusive relationship before seeking support from Grace Foundation, a charitable trust providing accommodation and rehabilitation services.

She said she had been sober for five months and was working towards a better future for herself and her baby.

Before seeking help, she had spent time sleeping in stolen cars and abandoned houses when she was only 12 years old up until she was 16.

"I felt neglected and broken. I didn't grow up with my parents."

A key kaupapa of this year's World Homeless Day was 'What does Home mean or look like to you?' RNZ / Layla Bailey-McDowell

Morgan-Neal said losing touch with her Māori culture while growing up had also affected her, but reconnecting through pōwhiri, wānanga and kapa haka at Grace Foundation had been an important part of her journey.

She said the support helped her rebuild trust and focus on herself and her child.

"I didn't want to give my baby the life that I had. I wanted to give him better."

For her, a safe home had "healthy connections, love, caring ... and respecting and loving one another".

"Connecting with one another. That's what I think home is."

Her message to others experiencing similar challenges and addiction was to reach out for support.

"Change can happen. Change is worth it. Reach out for help. Speaking up is not wrong."

Manaaki Rangatahi chief executive Bianca Johanson is calling for more youth housing and a national strategy to address youth homelessness. RNZ / Coco Lance

Home is more than a roof

Community Housing Aotearoa's most recent report on severe housing deprivation found Māori made up 28.8 percent of people

experiencing homelessness, despite accounting for 17.1 percent of the population.

Pacific people accounted for 22.6 percent of those experiencing homelessness, despite making up about 8 percent of the population.

The report also highlighted the scale of youth homelessness, with more than half of people experiencing homelessness under the age of 24.

It warned youth homelessness could become a pathway into adult homelessness without early, age-appropriate support and changes to barriers that prevent young people accessing housing.

The World Homeless Day art exhibition by Kākano Youth Arts Collective reflects the lived experiences of rangatahi, capturing journeys from a “trap house to a home”. RNZ / Layla Bailey-McDowell

21-year-old Georgia, a member of Kākano Youth Arts Collective, said youth homelessness could be difficult to recognise because many young people were not sleeping on the street.

She had supported someone close to her who moved between homes, including a period when they slept together on a mattress in a garage.

"Just because you don't see youth on the street begging for change or sleeping in a blanket on the street doesn't mean it doesn't exist," she said.

"Youth homelessness is quite often jumping from couch to couch, staying at friends' houses, sleeping on horrible mattresses in people's garages."

Georgia said young people could end up staying in unsafe environments because they had nowhere else to go.

"It's quite a dangerous situation to be in, but you're so desperate to be somewhere that's not your own home because you don't want to be in your own home."

She said the lack of visibility meant youth homelessness could be pushed aside, even when young people were experiencing significant housing insecurity.

"Just because they're in a house doesn't mean they're actually safe, and that still classes as homeless because if you're couch surfing, it's not stable."

20-year-old youth advocate Platinum says homelessness goes beyond sleeping rough, with many rangatahi couch surfing or living in unsafe homes. RNZ / Coco Lance

Platinum, a 20-year-old rangatahi MC at the event, reiterated that homelessness was much broader than sleeping rough, with many young people moving between houses or living in unsafe environments.

"Homelessness is just an umbrella word for so many things. Homelessness is when you live in a house that has way too many people. Homelessness is when you are couch surfing, going from home to home," she said.

"People aren't choosing to be homeless."

Platinum said a home should be a safe place where people felt protected, heard and seen.

"Home isn't just a place, it's a life."

Manaaki Rangatahi is calling for greater investment in youth housing and a coordinated national response to homelessness.

World.title: Otago dominate Hawke's Bay on home turf, earning spot in NPC semifinals
World.content:
Otago got their revenge over Hawke's Bay and continued to defend their home ground fortress with a 50-14 win in their NPC quarter-final in Dunedin.

Earlier this season, Hawke's Bay pulled off a come from behind victory over the southerners but could not do the same on Saturday with a place in the semifinals on the line.

Otago made their intentions clear early with no.8 Christian Lio-Willie powering over from the back of a scrum to open the scoring in the seventh minute.

The home side had doubled their lead when halfback Kieran McClea marked his return to the starting lineup with a try in the 16th minute.

Hawke's Bay replied through their halfback Folau Fakatava, when he finished off a break from winger Nic Benn, but Otago restored their lead through tighthead prop Saula Ma'u who crashed over after some strong work from his forwards and took a 24-7 lead into halftime.

After the break Henry Bell extended the lead when he also scored off the back of a maul.

The visitors were awarded a penalty try and Joseva Tamani was sent to the sinbin for playing the ball on the ground and preventing Fakatava scoring his second in the 50th minute.

However, the home side could not be slowed down as Sam Nemec-Vial sprinted in to score, even though his team were still down to 14 men.

Replacement back Joel Lam scored his first try of the season as Otago kept piling on the points.

Hawke's Bay made mass changes on the hour mark but could not turn around their fortunes.

Otago's final try came after a couple of players came close but it was Harry Irving who got the ball down over the line.

The win also reinforced Otago's strength on their home ground, with a record of one loss in their last 12 games at Forsyth Barr Stadium.

World.title: Zach Bates qualifies on pole for Bathurst 1000
World.content:
Supercars rookie Zach Bates — not qualifying king Brodie Kostecki — will start the Bathurst 1000 in pole position.

Kostecki was on track to become the first driver to snare four straight pole positions after laying a mighty lap of two minutes and 4.4912 seconds as the fifth driver in Saturday's top-10 shootout.

Proven race winners Will Brown, David Reynolds and Anton De Pasquale tried, but failed to beat Kostecki's time.

But provisional pole-sitter Bates refused to waver, proving his mettle as the last driver with a searing lap around the famous Mount Panorama track.

Bates denied Kostecki with a scorching lap of Mt Panorama. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone )

A day after becoming the fastest Gen3 racer, the 22-year-old clocked 2:04.2062 to deny Kostecki by 0.285 seconds.

Bates had earlier become the first to go below the 2:04 benchmark in the Gen3 era after taking provisional pole with a time of 2:03.9376.

In just his second pursuit of the holy grail of Australian motorsport, Bates is the third rookie to claim pole position after Klaus Ludwig (1987) and Marcos Ambrose (2001).

The Canberra local is the son of former rally and Supercars driver Rick Bates, and the nephew of four-time Australian Rally champion Neal Bates.

His surprise success comes after his mother Alison Drower died from cancer weeks before his Bathurst 1000 debut last year, in which he finished 10th as part of the Triple Eight Race Engineering wildcard with the great Craig Lowndes.

Team 18 driver De Pasquale will start in the second row with fourth-fastest Cooper Murray, while series leader Matt Payne was 10th.

But Grove Racing star Payne will be far from disheartened, given he had started from 18th en route to last year's epic wet-weather triumph with former co-driver Garth Tander.

Reynolds will start on the grid in eighth after a family of ducks threatened to derail his bid for a second Bathurst 1000 title.

Tickford co-driver Mark Winterbottom was forced to a sudden halt when ducks were spotted crossing the track at Conrod Straight during practice on Friday.

Brock inspires Bathurst 20 years on Just as he does every year, Craig Lowndes is drawing on memories of Australian motorsport legend Peter Brock to fuel yet another attempt at the Bathurst 1000.

Winterbottom's sudden braking caught out Reynolds' co-driver James Courtney, who locked up and slammed into the rear of the Tickford Ford Mustang.

But both cars were able to return to complete the 60-minute practice session before the shootout.

Defending Supercars champion Chaz Mostert was among the big names to miss out on the top-10 shootout and will start from 16th for the best qualifying result in the Toyota Supra.

Payne's teammate Kai Allen fell agonisingly short in 11th, while title contender Broc Feeney was 12th ahead of Cam Waters in 13th.

Kostecki's rookie teammate Rylan Gray will start from the back row with Ryan Wood after the duo crashed out in separate incidents in Friday's first practice session.

ABC Sport will have a live blog of the Bathurst 1000 from lights out to the chequered flag on Sunday, October 11.

World.title: Light strikes again, ending play early after Renshaw's career-best knock
World.content:
Matt Renshaw has notched his career-high Test score to lead Australia into a healthy spot on day two of the first Test against South Africa in Durban.

Renshaw's 190 eclipsed his previous best from way back in January 2017 and carried the team from 6-124 to 390 all out by the time he nicked off two balls after tea.

Renshaw was supported in an 86-run partnership with Pat Cummins (43 off 98) that was eclipsed by a marathon 134-run stand with Nathan Lyon (27 off 92), which stands as Australia's second-best stand for the ninth wicket in Test history.

Australia's bowlers wasted no time making an impact in their primary role as Josh Hazlewood removed South Africa opener Ryan Rickelton for a duck with the ninth ball of the innings.

Aiden Markram played some glorious drives to be unbeaten on 15 alongside David Bedingham, who was 12 not out at stumps.
